div.p: I have set down for you, in two books, an account of those who, though they pursued philosophy, were reputed to be sophists, together with those who were sophists properly so called. I do this knowing that you yourself are connected by descent with the art, since your lineage goes back to Herodes the sophist; and I remember, too, the discussions we once held together at Antioch, in the temple of Apollo at Daphne, concerning the sophists. As for their fathers, I have not, by Zeus, recorded them in every case, but only the fathers of men sprung from distinguished families. For I know that even Critias the sophist was mentioned with reference to his father only in the single case of Homer, since there was a marvel to be revealed in the fact that Homer was the son of a river. And in any case it is no profit to a man who wishes to know much that he should have at his fingertips the father and mother of this man or that, while remaining ignorant of the man's own virtues and vices, and of what he achieved and where he failed, whether through fortune or through his own judgement. This composition of mine, best of proconsuls, will lighten the burdens of your mind as well, just as the bowl of Helen, with its Egyptian drugs, lightened sorrow. Farewell, leader of the Muses.

praef. The ancient sophistic must be regarded as a rhetoric that philosophizes. For it discourses upon the same subjects as the philosophers; but whereas they, sitting in wait with their questions and advancing little by little through the small points of their inquiries, declare that they do not yet have knowledge, the ancient sophist speaks of these matters as one who knows. At any rate he makes the openings of his speeches with such phrases as "I know," and "I am aware," and "I have long since considered," and "nothing is certain for man." Such a manner of opening rings out at the very start a nobility in the speeches, and a high spirit, and a clear grasp of reality. This style is akin, on the one hand, to the human art of divination, which the Egyptians and Chaldeans, and before them the Indians, composed, conjecturing reality by means of countless stars; and on the other to the oracular and prophetic kind. For one may indeed hear the Pythian god say, "I know the number of the sand and the measures of the sea," and "Wide-seeing Zeus grants a wooden wall to the Tritan-born," and "Nero, Orestes, Alcmaeon, slayers of their mothers," and much of the same kind, speaking like a sophist.

Eudoxus of Cnidus, although he had given much careful thought to the discussions of the Academy, was nonetheless enrolled among the sophists for the elegance of his delivery and his skill in extempore speaking; and he was held worthy of the title of sophist throughout the Hellespont and the Propontis, and at Memphis and in the Egypt beyond Memphis, which Ethiopia bounds, and where dwell the Naked Sages of that country.

Concerning Herodes the Athenian the following must be known. The sophist Herodes belonged by descent to those who had twice held the consulship, and he traced his lineage back to that of the Aeacidae, whom Greece once made her allies against the Persian; nor did he disdain to count Miltiades and Cimon among his forebears, as men most excellent and of great worth to the Athenians and the other Greeks in the Median wars; for the one began the trophies over the Medes, and the other exacted from the barbarians the penalty for the outrages they later committed. He made the best use of wealth of all men. Let us not consider this an easy thing to manage, but among the most difficult and troublesome, for those who are drunk with wealth pour out insolence upon their fellow men. Men also slander wealth as blind; but though at other times it seemed blind, in the case of Herodes it recovered its sight: for it looked toward friends, it looked toward cities, it looked toward nations, since the man kept watch over all and stored up his wealth in the goodwill of those who shared in it. For he used to say that one who rightly uses wealth ought to relieve the needy so that they may not be in need, and to relieve those who are not in need so that they may not fall into need; and he called wealth that does not circulate and is restrained by stinginess "dead wealth," and the storerooms in which some lay away their money "prisons of wealth," and those who think they must even sacrifice to their hoarded money he named "Aloadae," who sacrificed to Ares after binding him.

The sources of his wealth were many and from many houses, but the greatest were that on his father's side and that from his mother. For his grandfather Hipparchus had his property confiscated on charges of aspiring to tyranny, charges that the Athenians did not bring, but that the emperor did not overlook; yet Fortune did not look on while Atticus, that man's son and the father of Herodes, was made poor from rich, but revealed to him an immeasurable treasure in one of the houses he possessed near the theatre. And, becoming through its very size more cautious than overjoyed, he wrote to the emperor a letter composed thus: "A treasure, O Emperor, I have found in my own house; what then do you command concerning it?" And the emperor — Nerva was then reigning — said, "Use what you have found." But when Atticus remained in the same caution and wrote that the measure of the treasure was beyond him, the emperor said, "Then make full use of your windfall, for it is yours." From this Atticus became great, but Herodes greater; for besides his father's wealth, his mother's wealth too, not much less than this, flowed in upon him.

There was a brilliant magnanimity in this Atticus too. For Herodes was governor of the free cities of Asia, and seeing that the Troad was badly off for baths and that the people drew earthy water from wells and dug cisterns for rainwater, he wrote to the emperor Hadrian not to overlook an ancient city, conveniently placed for the sea, perishing of drought, but to grant them three million for water, of which he had already given many times as much even to villages. The emperor praised the proposal as suited to his own character and put Herodes himself in charge of the water. But when the cost rose to seven million, and those who administered Asia wrote to the emperor that it was a monstrous thing that the tribute of five hundred cities should be spent on the fountain of a single city, the emperor reproached Atticus with this; and Atticus, most magnanimous of men, said, "O Emperor, do not be vexed over small matters; for what has been spent beyond the three million, I bestow upon my son, and my son bestows it upon the city." And his will too, in which he left to the people of the Athenians a mina to each man every year, attests the magnanimity of the man, which he displayed in other matters as well: sacrificing a hundred oxen to the goddess often in a single day, and feasting the people of the Athenians at the sacrifice by tribes and clans; and whenever the Dionysia came round and the image of Dionysus descended to the Academy, he gave drink to townsmen and strangers alike, as they reclined upon couches of ivy in the Cerameicus.

Since I have mentioned the will of Atticus, I must also record the reasons why Herodes fell out with the Athenians. The will ran, as I said, but he had written it on the advice of the freedmen about him, who, seeing the harsh nature of Herodes toward freedmen and slaves, made a refuge of the people of the Athenians, as though they themselves were responsible for the bequest. And what the freedmen's conduct toward Herodes was, let the indictment make plain which he composed against them, raising every sting of his tongue. When the will was read, the Athenians came to an agreement with Herodes that, by paying each of them five minas once for all, he should buy from them release from giving it always; but when they came to the banks for what had been agreed, and contracts of their fathers and grandfathers were read out against them as owing money to the parents of Herodes, they were drawn into counter-reckonings, and some were paid little, some nothing, while some were detained in the market-place as though they were even to pay. This exasperated the Athenians as men robbed of the bequest, and they did not cease to hate him even when he thought he was doing them the greatest benefits. So they said that the stadium was rightly named "Panathenaic," for it had been built out of what all the Athenians had been deprived of.

And indeed he performed the public services for the Athenians, both the eponymous and that of the Panhellenia, and when he was crowned in the office of the Panathenaea, he said, "I will receive you, men of Athens, and those of the Greeks who shall come, and the athletes who shall compete, in a stadium of white marble." And having said this, he completed within four years the stadium above the Ilissus, constructing a work beyond all the wonders, for no theatre rivals it. And I heard these things too about these Panathenaea: that a robe was hung upon the ship, more pleasing than any painting, its fold swelling with a fair wind, and that the ship ran not drawn by beasts of burden but gliding upon underground machinery, and that, setting out from the Cerameicus with a thousand oars, it was let go to the Eleusinium and, rounding it, passed by the Pelasgicum and, being conveyed past the Pythium, came to where it now is moored. The other end of the stadium holds a temple of Fortune and an ivory image as of one who steers all things. He also remodelled the Athenian ephebes to their present fashion, being the first to clothe them in white cloaks, for before this they used to sit through the assemblies wearing black, and to send the processions, while the Athenians publicly mourned the herald Copreus, whom they themselves killed when he was dragging the Heraclidae from the altar. Herodes dedicated to the Athenians also the theatre in memory of Regilla, constructing its roof of cedar — and this wood is precious also in the carving of statues. These two works, then, are at Athens such as exist nowhere else in the Roman empire. Worthy of mention too is the roofed theatre that he built for the Corinthians, far inferior to the one at Athens, but among the few that are praised among others; and the statues at the Isthmus, both the colossus of the Isthmian god and that of Amphitrite, and the rest, with which he filled the temple, not passing over the dolphin of Melicertes. He dedicated also to the Pythian god the stadium at Pytho, and to Zeus the water at Olympia, and to the Thessalians and the Greeks about the Malian gulf the swimming baths at Thermopylae, healing for the sick. He resettled too Oricum in Epirus, which had already declined, and Canusium in Italy, supplying it with water, of which it had much need; and he benefited the cities in Euboea and the Peloponnese and Boeotia, one in one way, another in another.

And though he was so great in great works, he thought he had accomplished nothing great because he had not cut through the Isthmus, considering it a brilliant thing to sever a continent and to join two seas and to cut short the lengths of a sea voyage of twenty-six stades. This he longed for, but did not dare to ask of the emperor, lest he should be slandered as seeming to lay hold of a project to which not even Nero had been equal. But he let it out in this way. For, as I heard from Ctesidemus the Athenian, Herodes was driving the road to Corinth with Ctesidemus seated beside him, and when he came to the Isthmus he said, "Poseidon, I wish it, but no one will allow it." Ctesidemus, marvelling at the saying, asked him the reason for his words. And Herodes said, "I have for a long time been contending to leave behind for the men after me a sign of a purpose that proves the man, and I do not yet think I have attained this glory." Ctesidemus then went on to recount praises of his words and his works, as having no surpassing by another; but Herodes said, "These things you speak of are perishable, for they are captured by time, and others break into our speeches as into a house, one finding fault with this, another with that; but the cutting of the Isthmus is an immortal work, and one that nature refuses to believe; for it seems to me that the breaking through of the Isthmus needs a Poseidon rather than a man."

The man whom the many called "the Heracles of Herodes" was a youth in the first down of his beard, equal to a great Celt and eight feet in height. Herodes describes him in one of his letters to Julianus: that his hair was moderately long, and his eyebrows shaggy and meeting one another as if they were one; that a gleaming ray came from his eyes, betokening a certain impulsive character; that he was hook-nosed and well-fleshed of neck, and that this came to him from toils rather than from food. He says too that his chest was firmly built and gracefully spare, and his shin slightly bowed outward, providing his step with a sure footing. He was clothed in the skins of wolves, a stitched garment, and he made his contests the wild boars and the jackals and the wolves and the bulls that run riot, and he used to show the wounds of these contests. As to this Heracles, some say he was earth-born in the Boeotian deme, but Herodes says he heard him say that his mother was a woman so strong that she herded cattle, and that his father was Marathon, whose image is at Marathon, a hero who is a husbandman. And Herodes asked this Heracles whether he was also immortal, and he said, "I am longer-lived than a mortal." He asked him too what he ate, and he said, "I eat milk-food for the greater part of the time, and goats nourish me, and shepherds, and the dams of the cattle and the horses; the udder of asses too yields a milk good to drink and light, and whenever I take to barley meal I eat ten quarts, and the Marathonian and Boeotian husbandmen bring me this contribution, who also name me Agathion, since I seem to them a man of good omen." "And how," said Herodes, "were you taught your speech, and by whom? For you do not appear to me to be one of the uneducated." And Agathion said, "The interior of Attica is a good schoolhouse for a man who wishes to converse; for the Athenians in the city, hiring Thracian and Pontic lads and youths flowed together from other barbarian nations, have their speech corrupted by them rather than contributing anything to their good utterance; but the interior, being unmixed with barbarians, keeps its speech sound, and its tongue rings out the purest Attic." "And were you present at a festival?" said Herodes. And Agathion said, "At Pytho, at least, not mingling with the crowd, but listening from a lookout point on Parnassus to the contestants in music, when Pammenes was admired for tragedy; and the wise Greeks seemed to me to be doing no good thing in listening with pleasure to the woes of the Pelopidae and the Labdacidae, for tales not disbelieved are counsellors of wretched deeds." Herodes, seeing that he was given to philosophy, asked him too how he regarded athletic contests, and he said, "I laugh at them the more when I see men contending with one another in the pancratium and boxing and running and wrestling, and being crowned for it; let the runner be crowned for outstripping a deer or a horse, and let the man who trains in the heavier events be crowned for grappling with a bull or a bear — what I do every day, since Fortune has robbed me of a great contest, for Acarnania no longer rears lions." So Herodes, full of admiration, begged him to dine with him. And Agathion said, "Tomorrow I will come to you at midday to the temple of Canobus, and let there be ready for you the largest bowl in the temple, full of milk that no woman has milked." And he came on the next day at the hour he had agreed, but, pressing his nose to the bowl, he said, "The milk is not pure, for a woman's hand assails me." And having said this he went away without touching the milk. So Herodes, giving heed to the saying about the woman, sent to the farms those who should investigate the truth, and learning that it was so, understood that there was a divine nature about the man.

Those who frame an accusation that the hands of Herodes were laid upon Antoninus on Mount Ida, at the time when the one governed the free cities and the other all the cities of Asia, seem to me to be ignorant of the trial of Demostratus against Herodes, in which, though he slandered him in very many ways, he nowhere mentioned this drunken violence, since it never happened. For a jostling did indeed befall them, as in a difficult and narrow place, but the hands committed no offense; so Demostratus would not have failed to recount it in his suit against Herodes, when he attacked the man so bitterly as even to slander what was praised in him. A charge of murder too came against Herodes, framed thus: that his wife Regilla was pregnant, in about her eighth month, and that Herodes, over no great matter, ordered Alcimedon, his freedman, to beat her, and that the woman, struck in the belly, died in an untimely birth. On these charges, as though true, Bradua, the brother of Regilla, indicts him for murder — a man most distinguished among the consuls and wearing the symbol of his noble birth attached to his shoe, this being a crescent-shaped ivory ankle ornament. And coming forward into the Roman senate, he set forth nothing convincing about the charge he was bringing, but made a long speech in praise of himself concerning his lineage; on which account Herodes, mocking him, said, "You have your nobility in your anklebones." And when the accuser boasted greatly even over a benefaction done to one of the cities of Italy, Herodes most nobly said, "I too could recount many such things about myself, if I were being tried in the whole earth." There assisted him in his defense, first, that he had ordered no such thing against Regilla, and next, that he mourned excessively at her death; for these things too were slandered as fiction, but nonetheless the truth prevailed. For he would never have dedicated to her such a theatre, nor postponed for her the second allotment of the consular office, had he not been clear of the charge; nor would he have dedicated her ornament to the temple at Eleusis, carrying it there defiled by murder, for this would have made the goddesses avengers of the murder rather than reconcilers. He also altered the very fashion of his house in her honor, darkening the flowers of its rooms with hangings and colors and Lesbian stone — and this stone is gloomy and black. About this it is said that Lucius too, a wise man, set himself to advise Herodes, and when he could not persuade him to change it, mocked him. And it is worthwhile not to pass over this either, since it is deemed worthy of mention by serious men.

This man was in outward matters serious, but having philosophized with Musonius of Tyre, he was keen-sighted in his replies and pursued wit in season; and being on the closest terms with Herodes, he was with him when he was bearing his grief badly, and admonished him, saying such things as these: "Herodes, all sufficiency is bounded by the mean, and on this subject I have both heard Musonius discourse much and discoursed much myself, and I heard you too at Olympia praising it to the Greeks, when you bade the very rivers flow in the middle of their banks. But where now are these doctrines? For, fallen out of yourself, you do things worthy to be mourned, endangering your reputation and much else besides." And when he could not persuade him, he went off in vexation. And seeing boys at a fountain in the house washing radishes, he asked them whose the dinner was, and they said they were preparing it for Herodes. And Lucius said, "Herodes wrongs Regilla in eating white radishes in a black house." When Herodes heard this reported, he took away the gloom from his house, lest he should become a plaything of serious men. Of this Lucius the following too is marvellous. The emperor Marcus was devoted to Sextus the philosopher from Boeotia, frequenting him and going to his doors; and Lucius, who had just come to Rome, asked the emperor, as he was setting out, where he was going and for what; and Marcus said, "It is good even for an old man to learn; I am going, then, to Sextus the philosopher to learn what I do not yet know." And Lucius, raising his hand to heaven, said, "O Zeus, the king of the Romans, already growing old, hangs a tablet about his neck and goes to school, while my king Alexander died at thirty-two." Even what has been said suffices to show the manner in which Lucius philosophized, for these things are enough to make the man plain, as the taste makes plain the fragrant wine.

The grief over Regilla, then, was thus quenched; but the grief over Panathenais, his daughter, the Athenians soothed by burying her in the city and decreeing that the day on which she died should be struck out of the year. And when his other daughter, whom he called Elpinice, died too, he lay upon the floor, beating the earth and crying, "What shall I consecrate to you, my daughter? What shall I bury with you?" And Sextus the philosopher, happening to be by, said, "You will give great things to your daughter if you mourn her with self-control." He mourned his daughters with these excesses because he held his son Atticus in anger. For he was slandered to him as foolish and a poor scholar and dull of memory; at any rate, when the boy was unable to take in his first letters, the idea occurred to Herodes to rear with him twenty-four boys of the same age, named after the letters, so that in the boys' names the letters might of necessity be practised by him. He saw too that the boy was given to drink and foolishly in love, on which account, while still living, he uttered over his own estate that verse: "And one more, a fool, is left in the wide house"; and at his death he gave back to him his mother's property, but transferred his own house to other heirs. But this seemed to the Athenians inhuman, since they did not consider Achilles and Polydeuces and Memnon, his foster-sons, whom he mourned equally with his own children, because they were most fair and good, noble and fond of learning, and worthy of their upbringing with him. At any rate he set up statues of them hunting, and having hunted, and about to hunt — some in thickets, some in fields, some by springs, some beneath the shade of plane trees, not without inscriptions, but with curses upon anyone who should mutilate or move them, whom he would not have honored so much had he not known them worthy of praise. And when the Quintilii, while they governed Greece, blamed him over the statues of these youths as excessive, he said, "What difference does it make to you if I amuse myself with my little stones?"

His quarrel with the Quintilii began, as most say, at the Pythian festival, since they listened to the music with differing opinions; but as some say, from the jest made about them by Herodes to Marcus. For seeing that they were Trojans but were deemed worthy of great honors by the emperor, he said, "I blame even the Homeric Zeus, that he loves the Trojans." But the truer cause is this. These two men, when both governed Greece, were summoned to the assembly by the Athenians, who uttered the cries of men under tyranny against Herodes, signifying their distress and asking above all that what was said be conveyed to the imperial ears. The Quintilii, having taken offense at the people and having impulsively sent up what they had heard, Herodes declared he was being plotted against by them, as men stirring up the Athenians against him. For after that assembly Demostrati and Praxagorai and Mamertini and many others sprang up, taking the opposite political side to Herodes. And Herodes, indicting them as men who were uniting the people against him, brought them before the governor; but they slipped away secretly to the emperor Marcus, trusting both in the nature of the emperor, which was more democratic, and in the moment;

trusting both in the nature of the emperor, which was more democratic, and in the moment. For those whom he suspected Lucius, who had become his colleague in rule, of favoring, he would not permit Herodes either not to share in his favor. The emperor, then, was encamped among the Paeonian peoples, using Sirmium as his base of operations, and Demostratus and his party lodged near the imperial quarters, Marcus providing them with maintenance and often asking whether they needed anything. He had persuaded himself to be kindly disposed toward them, and was persuaded thereto by his wife and by his little daughter, who still lisped — for she especially, falling at her father's knees with many caresses, begged him to save the Athenians for her. But Herodes was lodging in a suburb, in which towers and half-towers had been built, and there had travelled abroad with him twin maidens close to the age of marriage, admired for their beauty, whom Herodes, having reared them from infancy, had made his cupbearers and cooks, calling them his little daughters and greeting them thus — these were the daughters of Alcimedon, and Alcimedon was a freedman of Herodes. As they slept in one of the towers, which was the strongest, a thunderbolt carried down by night killed them. By this calamity Herodes was driven out of his wits, and he came into the imperial court neither in his right mind and longing for death. For coming forward he set himself to slanders of the emperor, not even giving his speech the form which it was fitting for a man trained in such a style to use in handling his own bile, but with his tongue elbowed aside and bare he kept straining, saying, "This is the result of the hospitality of Lucius, whom you sent to me; therefore you judge me, gratifying a woman and a three-year-old child." And when Bassaeus, the man entrusted with the sword, told him that he was speaking death for himself, Herodes said, "My good man, an old man fears few things." Herodes, then, left the court having said this and having left much of the water suspended, but let us consider the conduct of this trial too among the things conspicuously philosophized by Marcus; for he did not knit his brows, nor turn his eye, as even an arbitrator would have done, but turning himself to the Athenians, he said, "Make your defense, men of Athens, even if Herodes does not allow it." And as he heard them making their defense, he was secretly pained at many things, but when an assembly of the Athenians was read out to him too, in which they appeared to attack Herodes as one who courted the rulers of Greece with abundant honey, and where indeed they had cried out, "Oh, bitter honey," and again, "Blessed are those who die in the plague," he was so shaken in his heart by what he heard that he was led to manifest tears. But since the defense of the Athenians contained an accusation both of Herodes and of his freedmen, Marcus turned his anger upon the freedmen, using as mild a punishment as was possible — for so he himself characterizes his own judgment — but upon Alcimedon alone he remitted the penalty, saying that the calamity over his children was sufficient for him. These things, then, were thus philosophized by Marcus.

Some inscribe him as exiled, though he was not exiled, and say that he dwelt at Oricum in Epirus, which he also colonized, that it might be a residence suited to his body. But Herodes dwelt in this place when he fell sick there and offered a sacrifice for recovery from his sickness; and to go into exile he was neither commanded nor did he endure it. And as a witness to this account I will make the divine Marcus. For after the affairs in Paeonia, Herodes lived in Attica about the demes dearest to him, Marathon and Cephisia, with the youth from everywhere hanging upon him, who, out of love for his discourses, came to Athens. And the emperor, making trial whether Herodes were harsh toward him because of what happened in the court, sent to him a letter containing not a defense, but a complaint, for he said he wondered why Herodes no longer wrote to him, although in former time he wrote so often that even three letter-carriers once came to him in a single day, hard upon one another's heels. And the emperor wrote to Herodes through more, and about more matters, mingling a marvellous character into the letter, of which I will set forth, drawing it out, the parts that bear upon my present account. The opening, then, of the letter was: "Greeting to me, dear Herodes." And having discoursed about the winter quarters of the war, in which he then was, and having lamented his wife, lately dead to him, and having said something too about the weakness of his body, he writes next: "And for you I pray health, and that you think of me as well disposed toward you, and that you do not consider yourself wronged if, having detected some of your people doing wrong, I used as mild a punishment as was possible against them. For these things, then, do not be angry with me; but if I have grieved you in anything, or grieve you, demand satisfaction from me in the temple of Athena in the city at the mysteries. For I vowed, when the war was most inflamed, to be initiated, and may it be with you as my initiator." Such was the defense of Marcus, and so kindly and vigorous. Who, then, would ever have addressed thus one whom he had surrounded with exile, or have commanded one worthy to be so addressed to go into exile?

There is a story that Cassius, who governed the East, was plotting revolution against Marcus, and that Herodes rebuked him in a letter composed thus: "Herodes to Cassius: You are mad." Let us consider this letter not merely a rebuke, but also the strength of a man who set the weapons of his judgment on the side of the emperor. The speech which Demostratus delivered against Herodes is held to be among the marvellous. The character of its style is single, for its gravity runs from the opening to the end of the speech; but the styles of its expression are many, and unlike one another, yet worthy of mention. Let it be granted that the speech also wins repute among the envious because of Herodes, since such a man was spoken ill of in it. But that Herodes was strong against revilings too will be shown by the things once said by him at Athens to Proteus the Cynic. For this Proteus was one of those who philosophized so boldly that he even threw himself into fire at Olympia, and he used to follow Herodes about, reviling him in a half-barbarous tongue. So Herodes, turning round, said, "So be it, you revile me; for what purpose, and in this manner?" And when Proteus pressed on with his abuse, he said, "We have grown old, you reviling me, I hearing it" — indicating, no doubt, that he heard, but laughed, from being persuaded that false revilings come no further than the hearing.

I will interpret too the style of the man, coming to the character of his speech. That he counted Polemo and Favorinus and Scopelianus among his teachers, and that he attended Secundus the Athenian, I have already said; and the critics of speeches with whom he kept company were Theagenes of Cnidus and Munatius of Tralles, and Taurus of Tyre on the doctrines of Plato. The harmony of his speech was sufficiently chastened, and its formidable power crept beneath rather than lay upon the surface; there was resonance with simplicity, and an echo of Critias, and conceptions such as another could not conceive, and a comic felicity of language not imported but arising from the matters themselves; and his speech was sweet and rich in figures and well-figured and wisely varying, and his breath was not vehement, but smooth and steady, and the whole style of his speech was like gold-dust shining beneath a river with silver eddies. For he applied himself to all the ancients, but to Critias he was even devoted, and he led him into the regard of the Greeks, who till then neglected and overlooked him. And when Greece cried out over him and called him one of the Ten, he was not overcome by the praise, great as it seemed, but most wittily said to those who praised him, "I am better than Andocides." Being the readiest learner of men, he did not neglect toil either, but studied even over the cup and by night in the intervals of his sleep, on which account the careless and slight men called him "the fattened orator." So one man is good in one thing, another better than another in another; for one is marvellous at improvising, another at working out a speech, but Herodes arranged everything best of the sophists, and gathered the pathetic not from tragedy alone, but also from human affairs. There are very many letters of Herodes, and discourses and diaries and handbooks, and choice flowers of the ancient learning culled in brief. Those who reproach him because, while still young, he broke down in a speech before the emperor in Paeonia, seem to me not to know that Demosthenes too, speaking before Philip, suffered the same; and that man, coming to Athens, demanded honors and crowns when Amphipolis was lost to the Athenians, but Herodes, when he suffered this, went to the Ister as though to throw himself in, so great was his desire to be renowned in speeches, that he assessed his failure at death.

He died, then, at about seventy-six, having become wasted away. And when he died at Marathon and had enjoined his freedmen to bury him there, the Athenians, snatching him with the hands of the ephebes, carried him to the city, every age going to meet the bier with tears and with cries of blessing, as much as children bereaved of a good father, and they buried him in the Panathenaic stadium, inscribing upon him this brief and yet ample epitaph: "Of Atticus, Herodes the Marathonian, of whom all these things are: he lies in this tomb, of good repute on every side." So much about Herodes the Athenian — some things said, others unknown to others.

The ancient sophistic, even when it set forth philosophical themes, used to treat them at full length and in detail. For it discoursed about courage, it discoursed about justice, about heroes and gods and how the form of the universe has been shaped. But the sophistic that came after it — which we should call not new, since it is ancient, but rather a second sophistic — sketched out the poor man and the rich man, the noblemen and the tyrants, and the themes assigned to particular names, to which history gives rise. The leader of the more ancient school was Gorgias of Leontini among the Thessalians; of the second, Aeschines son of Atrometus, who, after being driven from politics at Athens, took up his residence in Caria and Rhodes. And some handled their themes by rule of art, others in the manner of Gorgias, by inspiration.

Leon of Byzantium in his youth was a pupil of Plato, but when he came to manhood he was called a sophist, since he had a manifold command of speech and was persuasive in his replies. For when Philip was marching against the Byzantines, Leon went out to meet him and said, "Tell me, Philip, what has come over you that you begin a war?" And when Philip replied, "Your fatherland, the fairest of cities, led me on to fall in love with her, and that is why I have come to the doors of my beloved," Leon took him up and said, "Those who deserve to be loved in return do not come to the doors of their beloved with swords; for lovers have need not of weapons of war, but of music." And he set Byzantium free, Demosthenes having spoken much to the Athenians, but Leon little to Philip himself. And when this Leon was on an embassy to the Athenians, the city had now for a long time been in a state of faction and was governed against its own character; and when he came forward into the assembly, he provoked in them an unrestrained burst of laughter at his appearance, since he looked fat and excessively heavy in the belly. But, not at all disconcerted by the laughter, he said, "Why, men of Athens, do you laugh? Is it because I am stout and so big? I have a wife much stouter than I, and when we are of one mind a single couch holds us, but when we quarrel not even the whole house does." And the people of the Athenians came to unity, harmonized by Leon, who had wisely improvised to suit the moment.

My account calls me to the sophist Theodotus. Theodotus presided over the people of the Athenians too at the time when the Athenians fell out with Herodes, and he came to no open enmity with the man, but secretly worked against him, being clever at managing affairs; for indeed he was one of the men of the market-place. At any rate he was so mingled with Demostratus and his party that he even helped them with the speeches they were composing against Herodes. He presided also over the youth of the Athenians, the first to do so on the ten thousand from the emperor. And this is not yet worthy of mention, for not all who mount this chair are worthy of mention, but that, whereas Marcus appointed Herodes to judge the Platonists and those of the Stoa and those of the Peripatos and the followers of Epicurus himself, this man he himself, from the reputation about him, judged for the young, calling him a contestant in political speeches and a benefit to rhetoric. This man was a pupil of Lollianus, but not without a hearing of Herodes. He lived, then, more than fifty years, holding the chair for two, and the style of his speeches was sufficient both for the men of the courts and for those who play the sophist to excess.

As for the sources from which extempore eloquence flowed, some say it sprang first from Pericles, which is why Pericles too was held to be great in his speech; others trace it to Python of Byzantium, whom Demosthenes says he alone of the Athenians could withstand when he ran on bold and full of flow; others say that the invention of extempore speaking belongs to Aeschines, for he, having sailed from Rhodes to the court of Mausolus the Carian, charmed him with an improvised speech. But to my mind Aeschines, of all men, improvised most, both when going on embassies and rendering account of them, both as advocate and as public speaker, and that he left behind only those speeches that were composed in writing, so that he might not fall far short of the studied works of Demosthenes; whereas the extempore speech was first begun by Gorgias. For he, coming forward into the theatre of the Athenians, had the courage to say, "Propose your subjects," and was the first to utter this daring challenge, thereby indicating, no doubt, that he knew all things and could speak on any subject whatever, trusting to the moment. And it occurred to Gorgias to do this for the following reason. Prodicus of Ceos had composed a speech, and not a disagreeable one: Virtue and Vice, in the form of women, come to visit Heracles, the one arrayed in cunning and gaudy attire, the other dressed just as it chanced; and to Heracles, who was still young, they hold out, the one idleness and luxury, the other squalor and toils. To this speech, which was put together at considerable length, Prodicus gave paid performances, going about the cities and charming them in the manner of Orpheus and Thamyris, on which account he was held in high esteem among the Thebans, and in still higher among the Lacedaemonians, as one who taught these things for the benefit of the young. So Gorgias, mocking Prodicus for delivering stale matter that had been said over and over, gave himself up to the moment. Yet he did not escape envy. For there was at Athens a certain Chaerephon — not the one whom comedy called "the boxwood," for that man was sick in his blood from his studies, but the one I now speak of, who practised insolence and jeered shamelessly. This Chaerephon, mocking the earnestness of Gorgias, said: "Gorgias, why is it that beans inflate the belly but do not inflate fire?" Gorgias, not at all disturbed by the question, replied: "This I leave to you to investigate; but I have long known this — that the earth grows stalks of fennel for such men as you."

Dias of Ephesus had cast the anchor-cable of his philosophy from the Academy, but he was reckoned a sophist for the following reason. Seeing that Philip was harsh toward the Greeks, he persuaded him to make war against Asia, and he went among the Greeks and argued that they ought to follow Philip on his campaign; for it was a fine thing, he said, even to serve abroad in order to be free at home.

Renowned among the sophists is Aristocles too, from Pergamon, about whom I will set forth what I heard from my elders. This man belonged to the consular order, and having philosophized in the Peripatetic doctrines from boyhood to his prime, he flowed over into the sophists, frequenting Herodes at Rome when he was delivering extempore speeches. During the time when he philosophized, seeming squalid and rough in appearance and unkempt in dress, he became luxurious and rubbed off his squalor, and all the pleasures of lyres and flutes and good voice he introduced into his manner of life, as though they had come to his very doors; for in former time, being so chastened, he used not to go disorderly to the theatres or to their echo. While he was in high repute at Pergamon, with all the Greek world there hanging upon him, Herodes, sending all his own pupils to Pergamon, raised up Aristocles like a vote of Athena. The style of his speech was translucent and Atticizing, but more suited to conversing than to contending; for bile is absent from his speech, and impulses are brief, and his very Atticism, if tested against the tongue of Herodes, will seem to argue minutely rather than to be composed of resonance and ring. Aristocles died half-grey, just stepping into old age.

The Athenians, seeing the formidable cleverness of the sophists, used to exclude them from the law courts, on the ground that they overcame what was just by an unjust argument and prevailed against the straight and right. Hence Aeschines and Demosthenes used to charge each other with this — not as a reproach, but as something held in suspicion by the jurors; for in private each thought himself admired for it. And Demosthenes, if Aeschines is to be believed, used to boast to his friends that he had brought the jurors' votes round to whatever he himself pleased. As for Aeschines, I do not think he would have set forth among the Rhodians doctrines they did not yet know, unless he had practised them at Athens as well.

And Carneades the Athenian too was numbered among the sophists; for though his mind was equipped in the philosophical manner, he drove the force of his arguments to the extreme of formidable cleverness.

Antiochus the sophist was brought forth by Aegae of the Cilicians, so noble that even now his descendants are of consular rank. Being charged with cowardice because he did not come before the people, nor take part in public affairs, he said, "It is not you, but myself, I fear" — knowing, no doubt, that his own bile was unmixed and uncontrollable. But nonetheless he benefited his fellow citizens from his estate, as far as he was able, both giving grain whenever he perceived them to be in need of it, and money for the works that had fallen into decay. He passed most of his nights sleeping in the temple of Asclepius, both for dreams and for the kind of companionship that belongs to men awake and conversing with one another; for the god conversed with him while he was awake, making it a fine contest of his own art to ward off the diseases of Antiochus.

Antiochus was, as a boy, a pupil of Dardanus the Assyrian, but advancing to youth he became a pupil of Dionysius of Miletus, who already held sway over the Ephesians. He used to converse not aptly — but, being the most prudent of men, he slandered this as boyish, that he might appear to have looked down upon it rather than to have fallen short of it — but in declamation he was most distinguished; for he was secure in the themes brought forward in figured fashion, vehement in his accusations and onslaughts, comely in his defenses and strong in the ethical, and, in a word, his style of speech was more sophistical than forensic, and more forensic than sophistical. And he handled the passions best of the sophists, for he did not draw out monodies, nor underlying laments, but expressed them briefly with thoughts greater than speech, as is shown both by his other themes and most of all by these. A girl who had been violated has chosen the death of the man who violated her; afterward a child has been born of the violence, and the grandfathers contend on which side the child is to be reared. Contending, then, on behalf of the grandfather on the father's side, he said, "Give back the child, give it back now, before it tastes its mother's milk." And the other theme is this: A man who had laid down his tyranny on condition of immunity was killed by a eunuch who had been made such by him, and he makes his defense for the murder. Here he thrust aside the strongest point of the accusation — the argument about the treaty — mingling subtlety with the passion: "To whom," he said, "did he agree these things? To boys, women, lads, old men, men; but I have no name in the compact." And he made the best defense too on behalf of the Cretans, who were on trial over the tomb of Zeus, contending brilliantly with natural philosophy and all theology. His declamations he made extempore, but he cared also for studied works, as both others of his works show and most of all his history; for in it he made a display of diction and rhetoric, devoting himself also to the love of the beautiful. About the death of the man, some say he died at seventy, others not yet, and some at home, others elsewhere.

The ancients gave the name of sophist not only to those orators who were of surpassing and brilliant voice, but also to those philosophers who expounded their thoughts with fluent ease; and of these I must speak first, since, though they were not sophists, they were thought to be such and so came to bear this name.

I know too of Philostratus the Egyptian, who shared philosophy with the queen Cleopatra, but was called a sophist because he had adopted a panegyrical and ornate style of speech, consorting as he did with a woman to whom even the love of letters was a kind of luxury. Hence some made a parody upon him in this elegiac couplet: "Keep clear of the wrath of all-wise Philostratus, who, now that he has kept company with Cleopatra, is reported to be the man you see."

Alexander, whom the many surnamed "Clay-Plato," had as his fatherland Seleucia, a not undistinguished city in Cilicia, and as his father a man of the same name, most capable in the speeches of the market-place, and as his mother a woman of surpassing beauty, as the paintings interpret, and resembling the Helen of Eumelus; for there is painted by Eumelus a Helen such as to be a dedication of the Roman market-place. They say that others were in love with this woman, but conspicuously Apollonius of Tyana, and that she rejected the rest, but kept company with Apollonius out of desire for fine offspring, since he was more divine than men. In how many ways this is incredible has been clearly said in my work on Apollonius. Alexander was godlike and conspicuous with beauty, for his beard was curly and let down to a moderate length, his eye delicate and large, his nose well-proportioned, his teeth most white, his fingers long and well-suited to the rein of speech. And he had wealth too, spent upon pleasures that were not to be blamed.

Coming to manhood, he went on an embassy on behalf of Seleucia to Antoninus, and slanders went round against him, that he affected youthfulness in his appearance. And when the emperor seemed to attend less to him, Alexander raised his voice and said, "Attend to me, Caesar." And the emperor, provoked at him for using too bold a manner of address, said, "I am attending, and I understand you; for you are the man who dresses his hair and polishes his teeth and pares his nails and always smells of perfume." He spent most of his life studying at Antioch and Rome and Tarsus and, by Zeus, in all Egypt, for he came even to the ways of the Naked Sages.

The stays of the man at Athens were few, but not unworthy to be known. For he was going to the Paeonian peoples, summoned by the emperor Marcus, who was campaigning there and had given him the office of writing letters to the Greeks; and coming to Athens — and this is no moderate length of road for one driving from the East — he said, "Here let us bend our knee." And having said this he announced to the Athenians extempore speeches, as they longed to hear him. And hearing that Herodes was staying at Marathon, and that all the youth followed him, he wrote to him a letter asking for the Greeks, and Herodes said, "I will come with the Greeks, and I myself too." So they gathered in the theatre in the Cerameicus, which is named the Agrippeium; and as the day was already advancing and Herodes was late, the Athenians grew impatient, as though the hearing were being broken up, and they thought it a trick; on which account it became necessary for Alexander to come forward to his discourse even before Herodes arrived. The discourse, then, was praises of the city and a defense to the Athenians for not having come to them before, and it had a sufficient length, for it resembled an epitome of a Panathenaic oration. And he seemed to the Athenians so well-arrayed that a buzz ran through them, while he was still silent, as they praised his good appearance. The theme that won the victory was the man bringing the Scythians back to their former wandering, since dwelling in a city they fall sick; and waiting a brief moment he leaped up from the chair with a bright face, as though bringing good tidings to his hearers of what he had to say. As his speech was advancing, Herodes stood by, shading his head with an Arcadian felt hat, as he was wont to do at Athens in the season of summer, and perhaps also indicating to him that he had come from the road. And Alexander, taking it from there, discoursed upon the man's presence in language somewhat dignified and ringing, and left it to him whether he wished to hear the theme already being treated, or himself to give another. And when Herodes looked up at his hearers and said that he would do whatever seemed good to them, all assented to the hearing of the Scythians, for indeed he was going through the contest brilliantly, as what has been said shows. He displayed a marvellous strength in these things too: for the thoughts he had brilliantly expressed before Herodes arrived, he handled, when Herodes stood by, with such other language and other rhythms that to those hearing them a second time he did not seem to repeat himself. At any rate, the most admired of the things said before Herodes arrived — "even water stagnant becomes diseased" — he afterward, when Herodes stood by, with another power transformed and said, "And of waters the sweeter are those that wander." And these too are of Alexander's Scythians: "When the Ister froze they drove toward the south, but when it thawed they went toward the north, sound in body and not, as now, lying low. For what dreadful thing could a man suffer who follows the seasons?" And at the end of the speech, slandering the city as a stifling dwelling, he uttered upon all this: "But fling open the gates, I wish to breathe." And running up to Herodes and embracing him he said, "Feast me in return," and Herodes said, "Why should I not, when you have feasted me so brilliantly?" And when the hearing was dissolved, Herodes called the most advanced of his own pupils and asked them what sort of sophist the man seemed to them; and when Sceptus of Corinth said that he had found the clay, but was seeking Plato, Herodes, checking him, said, "Say this to no one else, for you will slander yourself as judging ignorantly; rather follow me, who consider him a sober Scopelianus." This Herodes said, having observed that the man fitted a blended style of expression to his boldness in sophistical conceptions. And displaying himself before Alexander, he raised the echo of his discourse, since he knew that this man rejoiced most of all in tone, and introduced into his speech rhythms more varied than flute and lyre, since the man seemed to him copious also in his variations. The theme that was treated was the wounded in Sicily begging the departing Athenians to be killed by them. On this theme he made that much-talked-of supplication, drenching his eyes with tears: "Yes, Nicias, yes, father; so may you see Athens." At which they say Alexander cried out, "Herodes, we sophists are all morsels of you"; and Herodes, overjoyed at the praise and become himself again, gave him ten beasts of burden, ten horses, ten cupbearers, ten shorthand writers, twenty talents of gold, and a very great deal of silver, and two children from Collytus who lisped, since he heard that he rejoiced in young voices. Such, then, was his conduct at Athens.

Since I have set forth the memorable sayings of other sophists too, let Alexander also be made plain from several, for he has not yet come to the fullness of his reputation among the Greeks. That he discoursed both with dignity and with pleasure, these of his discourses show: "Marsyas was in love with Olympus, and Olympus with flute-playing"; and again, "Arabia is a land of many trees, of shaded plains, with nothing bare; the plants are the earth, the flowers. You will not throw away a single Arabian leaf, nor cast off a single straw of anything grown there, so fortunate is the earth in its perfumes." And again, "A poor man from Ionia — and Ionia is Greeks settled in the land of the barbarians." Antiochus, mocking this style and spitting upon him as one luxuriating in the bloom of words, came forward at Antioch and discoursed thus: "Ionias, Lydias, Marsyases, follies, give me problems." The advantages he had in declamation have been shown by these too, but let them be shown by other themes as well. For going through Pericles, who bade them hold to the war even after the oracle in which the Pythian god said that, called and uncalled, he would fight on the side of the Lacedaemonians, he met the oracle thus: "But the Pythian, he says, promises to help the Lacedaemonians; he lies; for so he promised them Tegea too." And going through the man advising Darius to bridge the Ister: "Let the Ister of the Scythians flow beneath you, and if it carry your army across with a fair stream, honor it by drinking of it." And contending as Artabazus, who forbade Xerxes to march a second time against Greece, he spoke briefly thus: "The affairs of the Persians and Medes are such as I say, O king, if you remain in your land; but the affairs of the Greeks — a thin land, a narrow sea, men driven to desperation, and grudging gods." And persuading those who fell sick in the plains to move up to the mountains, he philosophized about nature thus: "It seems to me that even the maker of the universe flung down the plains, as the baser matter, but raised up the mountains, as dignities. These the sun greets first, and leaves last. Who will not love a place that has the longer days?" The teachers of Alexander were Favorinus and Dionysius; but from Dionysius he went away half-taught, summoned by his father, who was sick, when indeed he died, while of Favorinus he was a most genuine pupil, from whom most of all he drew the bloom of his speech. Of the death of Alexander some say it was in the land of the Celts while still writing letters, others in Italy when he had ceased writing letters; and some say at sixty, others not yet, and some that it was over a son, others over a daughter, about which I found nothing worthy of mention.
And Theomnestus of Naucratis, who was conspicuously a philosopher, was carried off among the sophists by the amplitude of his style.

Let Varus too, from Perge, be deemed worthy of mention. Varus had as his father Callicles, a man among the most powerful of the Pergaeans, and as his teacher Quadratio the consul, who improvised the thetic themes and played the sophist in the manner of Favorinus. The many surnamed Varus "the Stork," because of the redness of his nose and its beaklike shape; and that they jested at this not without reason one may gather from the statues that are set up in the temple of the Pergaean goddess. The character of his speech was such as this: "Coming to the Hellespont you ask for a horse, but coming to Athos you wish to sail. Do you not know, man, the ways? But having thrown a little earth upon the Hellespont, do you think this stays for you, when the mountains do not stay?" He was said to deliver these things in a brilliant and practised voice. He died at home, not yet grown old and leaving children, and his descendants are all of good repute in Perge.

As for Dio of Prusa, I do not know what one ought to call him, on account of his excellence in every kind; for he was, as the saying goes, a horn of Amalthea, compounded of the finest sayings of the finest authors. He kept his eye upon the resonance of Demosthenes and Plato, to which, like the bridges that resonate on instruments, Dio adds his own peculiar note with a deliberate simplicity. And what is best in Dio's speeches is the blending of character; for though he rebuked insolent cities most severely, he did not seem fond of railing, nor disagreeable, but as one who curbs the insolence of horses with the bridle rather than the whip; and when he set himself to praise well-governed cities, he did not seem to exalt them, but rather to bring them to their senses, as cities that would perish if they changed their ways. The character of the rest of his philosophy, too, was neither common nor ironical, but earnestly applied, yet tinged, as with a seasoning, with gentleness. That he was also capable of writing history is shown by his Getica; for indeed he went among the Getae when he was a wanderer. As for the Euboean discourse, and the Praise of the Parrot, and all the matters not of great moment that Dio took seriously, let us not consider them trivial, but sophistical; for it is the mark of a sophist to take pains even over such things as these.

Hermogenes, whom Tarsus brought forth, when he was fifteen years old advanced to so great a reputation among the sophists that he even provided the emperor Marcus with a desire to hear him. At any rate Marcus went to his hearing, and was pleased when he discoursed, and marvelled when he improvised, and gave brilliant gifts. But coming to manhood he was deprived of his power by no visible sickness, on which account he provided the envious with matter for a witticism, for they said that his speeches were simply, according to Homer, "winged," since Hermogenes had cast them off as if they were wings. And Antiochus the sophist, jeering at him once, said, "This is Hermogenes, who among boys was an old man, but among the aged a boy." The style of speech that he practised was somewhat of this kind: discoursing before Marcus, he said, "Behold, I come to you, O king, an orator in need of a tutor, an orator awaiting maturity," and he discoursed much else of this buffoonish sort. He died, then, in deep old age, but considered one of the many, for he was despised when his art deserted him.

Living in the times when Apollonius of Tyana and Euphrates of Tyre were practising philosophy, he was on friendly terms with both, although they were at variance with each other beyond what befits the philosophic character. His journey to the Getic peoples I do not think it right to call an exile, since he was not commanded to go into exile, nor yet an absence abroad, since he withdrew from public view, stealing himself away from eyes and ears and doing now one thing in one land, now another in another, out of fear of the tyrannies then ruling in the city, by which all philosophy was being driven out. And while he planted and dug and drew water for baths and gardens and did much other such work for the sake of his livelihood, he did not neglect his studies, but kept himself together by means of two books; and these were the Phaedo of Plato and the speech of Demosthenes On the Embassy. Frequenting the camps, where he was wont to wear himself out, and seeing the soldiers rushing toward revolt upon the murder of Domitian, he did not hold back when he saw disorder breaking out, but, leaping up naked upon a high altar, he began his speech thus: "Then resourceful Odysseus stripped off his rags"; and when he had said this and made it plain that he was no beggar, nor the man they supposed, but Dio the wise, he breathed mightily in his accusation of the tyrant, and taught the soldiers to think more wisely in doing what was approved by the Romans. For indeed the persuasiveness of the man was such as could charm even those who were not versed in the affairs of the Greeks. Trajan the emperor, at any rate, having seated him beside himself at Rome in the golden chariot in which the emperors ride in triumphal procession after their wars, would often turn round to Dio and say, "What you are saying I do not know, but I love you as I love myself." Most sophistical of all in Dio are the images in his speeches, in which, though he is copious, he is also vivid and faithful to his subjects.

In like manner the eloquence of Favorinus the philosopher proclaimed him among the sophists. He was one of the Gauls of the West, from the city of Arelate, which is settled upon the river Eridanus. He was born of double nature, both man and woman, and this was shown both by his appearance — for even as he grew old he remained beardless of face — and by his voice, which was heard to be shrill and thin and high-pitched, such as nature has fashioned for eunuchs. Yet he was so ardent in matters of love that he was even charged with adultery by a man of consular rank.

Philagrus the Cilician was a pupil of Lollianus, and the most fiery and most choleric of the sophists; for it is said that he once struck a hearer who was nodding off on the cheek. And having from boyhood used a brilliant impulse, he was not deprived of it even when he grew old, but advanced so far in it that it was even considered a fashion set by the teacher. Having mingled with very many nations and seeming to handle his themes best, he did not handle his own bile well at Athens, but brought himself into enmity with Herodes, as though he had come for this purpose. For he was walking in the afternoon in the Cerameicus with four others, of the sort at Athens who hunt the sophists, and seeing a young man turning from the right with several others, and thinking himself mocked by him, he said, "Surely you are someone?" "I am Amphicles," he said, "if indeed you have heard of the Chalcidean." "Keep away, then," he said, "from my hearings, for you do not seem to me to be in your right mind." And when the other asked, "And who are you to proclaim this?" Philagrus said, "It is a dreadful thing to suffer, to be anywhere unknown." But when an outlandish phrase escaped him as in anger, Amphicles caught at it — for indeed he happened to hold the first place among the pupils of Herodes — and said, "In which of the distinguished men is this phrase found?" And he said, "In Philagrus." This drunken violence, then, advanced to such things; and on the next day, learning that Herodes was staying in the suburb, he wrote him a letter attacking the man as neglecting the orderliness of his hearers. And Herodes said, "You seem to me not to open well," rebuking him as not gaining the goodwill of hearers, which one ought to consider the opening of displays. And he, as though not understanding the riddle, or understanding it but setting in jest the judgment of Herodes, which was best, was deceived of his display, coming forward before hearers who were not well-disposed.

Though a quarrel arose between him and the emperor Hadrian, he suffered no harm. Hence, as though they were marvels, he used to recite, like oracles, these three things about his own life: that, being a Gaul, he spoke Greek; that, being a eunuch, he was tried for adultery; that he had quarrelled with an emperor and yet lived. But this would rather be to the credit of Hadrian, if, being emperor, he quarrelled on equal terms with a man whom he had power to put to death. "A king is the stronger when he is wroth with a meaner man" — provided he masters his anger; and "great too is the wrath of kings nurtured by Zeus" — provided it is chastened by reason. It is better that those who would set the characters of kings in a good light should ascribe such sayings to the opinions of the poets. When Favorinus had been appointed high priest in his native city, he sought, in accordance with the laws governing such matters, to be released from the public service, since he was a philosopher; but seeing that the emperor was minded to lay down the opposite opinion against him, on the ground that he was not a philosopher, he forestalled him thus: "A dream has come to me, O Emperor," he said, "which I ought to tell to you as well. For Dio my teacher stood beside me and admonished me concerning the suit, saying that we are born not for ourselves alone, but also for our fatherlands. I accept, then, O Emperor, the public service, and obey my teacher."

For, as I heard from my elders, his discourse gave offense, seeming new-sounding and with its conceptions strained, and it seemed too boyish, for a lament for a woman who had died on him in Ionia was mingled into his praises of the Athenians. And his declamation was plotted against thus. He had argued, in Asia, a theme — those declining the alliance of the uninvited; and this theme having already been published, he had committed it to memory, for indeed he happened to have won repute on it. And when word came to the party of Herodes that Philagrus improvised the themes that were defined for the first time, but those defined a second time no longer, but declaimed stale matter already spoken by himself, they proposed to him these "uninvited"; and as he seemed to improvise, his declamation was read out against him. And as much tumult and laughter held the hearing, Philagrus, shouting and crying out that he was suffering dreadfully, being kept from his own, did not escape the charge already believed. These things, then, happened in the Agrippeium; and after an interval of about four days he came forward into the council chamber of the artists, which is built by the gates of the Cerameicus not far from the cavalry. And while contending most brilliantly as Aristogeiton, who claims to accuse Demosthenes of Medism and Aeschines of Philippism, over which they happened to have indicted one another, his voice was quenched by his bile, which by nature darkens the voice of choleric men by darkening the breath of utterance. Some time later, then, he mounted the chair at Rome, but at Athens he was carried away from his reputation for the reasons I have said.

All this the emperor made into a kind of pastime, and he passed his royal cares by inclining toward sophists and philosophers; but to the Athenians it seemed a terrible thing, and they ran together — chiefly the Athenians in office — and threw down the bronze statue of the man as though he were a bitter enemy of the emperor. But Favorinus, when he heard of it, neither complained nor grew savage over the outrage done him, but said, "Socrates too would have profited had he been deprived of a bronze statue by the Athenians rather than have drunk hemlock." He was on the closest terms with Herodes the sophist, who regarded him as his teacher and father, and wrote to him, "When shall I see you, and when shall I kiss your lips all over?" And so, at his death, Favorinus declared Herodes heir to all the books he possessed, and to his house at Rome, and to Autolecythus. This last was an Indian and quite black, a plaything of Herodes and Favorinus; for he used to keep them entertained as they drank together, mingling Attic with Indian and stumbling into barbarisms with his blundering tongue. The quarrel that arose between Favorinus and Polemo began in Ionia, when the Ephesians attached themselves to him, since Smyrna admired Polemo; and it grew greater at Rome, for consuls and the sons of consuls, some praising the one, some the other, set them at rivalry, which kindles much envy even in wise men. They are pardonable, then, for their rivalry, since human nature counts ambition ageless; but they are to be blamed for the speeches they composed against each other, for licentious abuse, even if it happens to be true, does not free from disgrace even the man who has spoken about such matters. As for those who call Favorinus a sophist, the very fact that he quarrelled with a sophist suffices for proof; for that ambition I have mentioned makes its way against rivals in the same craft.

The character of Philagrus' speeches in his discourses was such as this: "Then do you think the sun envies the evening star, or cares if there is some other star in heaven? Not so are the affairs of this great fire. For it seems to me to apportion to each even poetically, saying, 'To you I give the Bear, to you the south, to you the evening; but all are in night, all, whenever I am not seen': 'The sun rose, leaving the most beautiful mere,' and the stars are nowhere." And what the rhythms of his declamation were, the things said to the uninvited will show — for he was said to bid them rejoice too: "Friend, today I have beheld you, and today you talk to me in arms and with a sword, and I know only the friendship that comes from the assembly. Go away, then, men, friends — for this name we keep for you — and if we ever have need of allies, we will send for you, if ever indeed."

His style was fashioned with a free looseness, yet wisely and refreshingly; and he was said to improvise with great fluency. The speech against Proxenus, I declare, Favorinus would neither have conceived nor composed, but it is the work of some drunken youth — or rather of one vomiting. But the speech on the man who died untimely, and the one on the gladiators, and the one on the baths, we pronounce genuine and well composed; and much more so the speeches of his that treat of philosophy, of which the best are the Pyrrhonian discourses; for the Pyrrhonists, although they suspend judgment, are not thereby deprived of the power to give judgment. When he discoursed at Rome, everything was full of eager attention; for indeed even those who had no understanding of the Greek tongue found his hearing no less a pleasure, since he charmed them too by the ring of his voice, by the expressiveness of his glance, and by the rhythm of his tongue. He charmed them also by that part of the speech which they called the "song," but which I call ambition, since it is sung as a finale to the proofs already given. He is said to have heard Dio, but he stands as far from him as those who never heard him at all. So much for those who, though philosophers, were reputed to be sophists. The men properly called sophists were the following.

Philagrus was less than moderate in stature, bitter of brow, ready of eye, and prompt to be called forth to anger, and he was not himself ignorant of the ill-temper in him; at any rate, when one of his companions asked him what made him take no joy in rearing children, he said, "Because I take no joy even in myself." Of his death some say it was at sea, others in Italy at the threshold of old age.

Sicily brought forth Gorgias at Leontini, to whom we should trace the art of the sophists, as to a father. For if we consider Aeschylus, how much he contributed to tragedy by equipping it with stage costume and the high buskin and the figures of heroes, with messengers and reporters and all that must be done on the stage and behind it, this is just what Gorgias was to his fellow craftsmen. For he was the originator, among the sophists, of the impulsive style, of paradox, of inspired loftiness, of expressing great themes greatly, of detachments and assaults, by which speech becomes sweeter than itself and more stately; and he clothed it too in poetic words for the sake of adornment and dignity. That he improvised most easily I have said at the beginning of my account; and when he discoursed at Athens, already an old man, if he was admired by the multitude, that is no marvel, but he won over, I think, even the most distinguished men: Critias and Alcibiades, who were then young, and Thucydides and Pericles, who were then growing old. Agathon too, the tragic poet, whom comedy knows as wise and elegant in speech, in many places of his iambics "Gorgianizes."

Aristides — whether the son of Eudaemon or himself Eudaemon — was brought forth by the Adriani, and the Adriani are a not great city among the Mysians; but Athens trained him in the prime of Herodes, and Pergamon in Asia in the time of the tongue of Aristocles. Being sickly from youth, he did not neglect toil. The kind of his sickness, and that his nerves shuddered, he himself relates in his Sacred Tales; and these books hold for him a certain place of diaries, and diaries are good teachers of speaking well on every subject. But as his nature did not follow him toward improvisation, he gave heed to precision and looked sufficiently to the ancients, and was strong in fertility, removing empty talk from his speech. The travels of Aristides were not many, for he neither discoursed to please the multitude nor mastered his bile against those who heard him without praise; but the nations he visited are Italians and Greece and the Egypt settled by the Delta, who set up a bronze statue of him in the market-place of Smyrna.

Distinguishing himself also at the festivals of the Greeks, he sounded forth his Pythian speech from the altar, where a golden statue of him was set up, in the temple of the Pythian god; while his Olympian speech was directed to the greatest of political ends. For, seeing Greece in a state of faction, he became a counsellor of concord to them, turning them against the barbarians and persuading them to make, not one another's cities, but the country of the barbarians, the prize of their arms. As for the funeral oration which he delivered at Athens, it was spoken over those who fell in the wars whom the Athenians buried at public expense with words of praise, and it is composed with surpassing wisdom; for while he urged the Athenians on against the Medes and Persians, and contended for the same end as in his Olympian speech, he said nothing about concord toward the Greeks, since he was addressing Athenians who loved empire, which could not be won unless they chose the path of action; instead he dwelt upon the praises of the trophies won over the Medes, showing them that trophies over barbarians call for hymns, but trophies over Greeks for dirges.

And to call Aristides the founder of Smyrna is no boastful praise, but most just and most true. For this city, having been destroyed by earthquakes and chasms, he so lamented to Marcus that the king often groaned over the rest of the monody, but at the words "and the west winds blow over her desolate" the king let tears drop upon the book and assented, from the cues given by Aristides, to a resettlement for the city. And Aristides happened to have met with Marcus already in Ionia; for, as I heard from Damianus the Ephesian, the emperor was already staying at Smyrna for the third day, and not yet knowing Aristides, he asked the Quintilii whether the man might have been overlooked by him in the throng of those who greeted him; and they said that they themselves had not seen him, for they would not have failed to introduce him, and on the next day they both came escorting Aristides. And when the emperor addressed him, he said, "Why have we been slow to see you?" And Aristides said, "A theory, O king, kept me busy, and a mind contemplating something must not be torn away from what it seeks." And the emperor, overjoyed at the man's character as most simple and most scholarly, said, "When shall I hear you?" And Aristides said, "Propose a theme today, and hear it tomorrow; for we are not of those who vomit, but of those who are precise. And let it be permitted, O king, that my pupils too be present at the hearing." "It is permitted," said Marcus, "for that is democratic." And when Aristides said, "And let it be granted to them, O king, both to shout and to applaud as much as they can," the emperor said with a smile, "That rests with you." I have not written the theme that was declaimed, since some say one, some another, but this much is agreed by all, that Aristides showed the best impulse before Marcus, Fortune from afar preparing the resettlement of Smyrna through such a man. And I do not say this as though the king too would not have resettled a city that had perished, which he admired while it stood, but because royal and divine natures, if counsel and speech rouse them, blaze up the more and are carried with impulse toward doing good.
Gorgias is said to have reached one hundred and eight years, and yet his body was not undone by old age; on the contrary, he lived to the end sound and with his senses still in their vigor.

I heard these things too from Damianus, that this sophist slandered the improvisers in his discourses, but so admired improvisation that he even worked at it privately, shutting himself up in a little room; and he worked it out, turning clause upon clause and thought upon thought. But let us consider this the work of one chewing rather than eating, for improvisation is the contest of a fluent tongue. Some accuse Aristides of having spoken a cheap opening in the case of the mercenaries from whom the land is demanded, for he began this theme thus: "These men will not cease providing us with trouble." Some lay hold too of a vigorous saying of the man in the case of the one declining the fortification of Lacedaemon, where he said: "Let us not cower in a wall, taking on the nature of quails." They lay hold too of a proverb as having been thrown in basely, for slandering Alexander as taking after his father, he said that the boy was his father's child in cleverness at affairs. The same men accuse him of a jest, since he said that the one-eyed Arimaspians were kinsmen of Philip, as though Demosthenes had made his defense to the Greeks over the "tragic ape" and the "rustic Oenomaus." But let us not judge Aristides from these things; rather let him be made plain by the Isocrates who leads the Athenians off the sea, and the one rebuking Callixeinus for not burying the Ten, and those deliberating about the affairs in Sicily, and the Aeschines who did not take the grain from Cersobleptes, and those declining the treaty after slaying the families — in which most of all the themes he teaches us how one might safely handle hazardous and tragic conceptions. And I know many other themes too that display the good education of this man, and his strength and character, from which he is rather to be regarded, than if somewhere he even spat out something, having fallen into ambition. And Aristides was the most artful of the sophists and copious in theoretical matters, on which account he was carried away from improvisation too; for to wish to advance everything according to theory occupies the mind and removes it from readiness. Of the death of Aristides some write that it was at home, others in Ionia; and as to his years, some say sixty, others near seventy.

Protagoras of Abdera the sophist was at home a pupil of Democritus, but he also consorted with the Magi from Persia during Xerxes' march against Greece.
