For his father was Maeander, a man furnished with wealth beyond most in Thrace, who, having received Xerxes with hospitality and gifts, procured for his son the company of the Magi from him; for the Persian Magi do not instruct any but Persians, unless the king grants it. Protagoras' saying that he could not tell whether the gods exist or do not exist seems to me to be a transgression that he derived from his Persian education; for the Magi invoke the divine in the rites they perform in secret, yet do away with the public belief in the divine, not wishing to seem to derive their power from it. For this reason he was driven by the Athenians out of every land, according to some after a trial, but as it seems to others, by a vote passed without his being tried. And as he passed from continents to islands, avoiding the Athenian triremes that were sown over every sea, he was drowned sailing in a small boat. He was the first to discover the practice of charging a fee for discourse, and the first to hand on to the Greeks a thing not to be blamed; for the things we study at expense we welcome more than those that come free. Plato, recognizing that Protagoras expounded his thoughts with dignity but lay back upon that dignity, and was here and there more long-winded than was fitting, characterized his manner in a long myth.

Adrianus the Phoenician was brought forth by Tyre, but trained by Athens. For, as I heard from my own teachers, he came to them in the time of Herodes, displaying a most sophistical strength of nature and not unclear that he would advance to greatness; for he frequented Herodes when about eighteen years old, perhaps, and being quickly deemed worthy of what Sceptus and Amphicles were deemed worthy, he was enrolled also in the hearing of the Clepsydrium. And the Clepsydrium was thus: ten of the hearers of Herodes who were deemed worthy of excellence used to feast in addition, after the hearing for all, on a water-clock measured to a hundred verses, which Herodes went through at length, having declined the praise of the hearers and become his own sole judge of his speaking. And as he had handed down to his pupils the rule of not relaxing even at the time of drinking, but of pursuing some study there too over the wine, Adrianus used to drink with those of the water-clock as a sharer in a great secret; and as a discussion advanced among them about the style of each of the sophists, Adrianus came forward into their midst and said, "I will sketch the characters, not remembering little phrases or trifling thoughts or clauses or rhythms, but setting myself to imitation and improvising the styles of all with fluency and giving rein to my tongue." And when he left out Herodes, Amphicles asked him why he passed over their teacher, when he himself was in love with his style and saw that they too were in love with it. And he said, "These men are such as to provide an imitation even to a drunken man, but Herodes the king of speeches it is enough for me to render if I act him sober and undrunken." When this was reported to Herodes it delighted him, who was in any case not above good repute. And Adrianus announced to Herodes a hearing of an extempore speech while still young, and Herodes —

And Adrianus announced to Herodes a hearing of an extempore speech while still young, and Herodes, not, as some slander, envying and jeering, but listening from a kindly and gracious disposition, strengthened the young man, saying upon all this, "These would be great fragments of a colossus" — at once correcting him as torn apart by his youth and not put together, and at once praising him as grand-voiced and grand-minded. And to Herodes when he died he pronounced a speech worthy of the man, so as to call the Athenians to tears at the hearing of the speech.

So full of frankness did he mount the chair at Athens that the opening of his discourse to them was not their wisdom, but his own, for he began thus: "Once again letters from Phoenicia." This opening, then, was of one breathing above the Athenians and giving them some good thing rather than receiving it; and he attended most magnificently to the chair at Athens, wearing clothing of great worth, hung about with the more marvellous stones, and going down to his studies on a chariot with a silver bridle, and, when he had studied, returning again enviable with a procession of the Greek world from everywhere. For these courted him as the clans of Eleusis court the hierophant brilliantly performing the rites. And he won them over too with games and drinking parties and hunts and the sharing of Greek festivals, being young with each in different things, on which account they were disposed toward him as children to a father, sweet and gentle and joining with them in the Greek frolic. Indeed I know that some of them even wept whenever they came to the memory of this man, and that some imitated his voice, some his walk, some the gracefulness of his dress.

A charge of murder too was brought against him, which he escaped thus. There was at Athens a little man not unexercised in the course about the sophists; to him if anyone brought a jar of wine, or dainties, or clothing, or money, he found him easy to handle, like those who lead the hungry of the flocks with a leafy branch, but if he were neglected, he was given to reviling and barked. He had given offense to Adrianus because of the easiness of his character, but he courted Chrestus the sophist from Byzantium; and Adrianus endured all that came from him, calling the revilings of such men "bug-bites," but his pupils, not enduring it, bade their own servants beat him, and his bowels swelling up, on the thirtieth day he died, providing some occasion himself too for his death, since being sick he drank unmixed wine. And the relatives of the dead man indict the sophist for murder before the governor of Greece, as one of the Athenians, since he had a tribe and deme at Athens; but the governor acquitted him of the charge, since he had struck neither with his own hands nor with those of his own slaves the man who was said to have died. There assisted him in his defense, first, the Greek world — for what cries did they not utter on his behalf, with tears withal? — and next, the testimony of the physician about the wine.

At the time when the emperor Marcus came to Athens for the mysteries, this man already held sway over the chair of the sophists, and Marcus made it part of his inquiry into the affairs of Athens not to be ignorant of his wisdom either; for indeed he appointed him to the young, not testing him by a hearing, but assenting to the report about him. And when Severus, a man of consular rank, slandered him as one who frenzied the sophistical themes, because he was strong in the contests, Marcus, making a proof of this, proposed to him the Hyperides who turns to the judgments of Demosthenes alone, when Philip was in Elatea; and he handled the contest so manageably that he was thought not even to fall short of the rush of Polemo. And the emperor, admiring him, raised him to greatness with privileges and gifts. By privileges I mean the maintenances and the front seats and the immunities and the priesthoods and whatever else makes men brilliant, and by gifts gold, silver, horses, slaves, and whatever expresses wealth, with which he filled both him and all his family.

And holding the upper chair too, he so turned Rome toward himself that he provided even those who had no understanding of the Greek tongue with a desire to hear him. And they listened as to a sweet-voiced nightingale, struck with his good utterance and his figure and the well-turned quality of his voice and his rhythms both in prose and with song. So whenever they were busy with the customary spectacles — and these are for the most part of dancers — if the announcer of his hearing appeared about the stage, they would rise from the senate, and rise from those who ride at public expense, not only those eager for Greek learning, but also as many as were taught the other tongue at Rome, and they went at a run to the Athenaeum, full of impulse and reviling those who walked at a pace.

When he was sick at Rome, when indeed he died, Commodus voted him the imperial correspondence with an apology that it had not come sooner, and he, invoking the Muses, as was his wont, and kissing the imperial tablets, gave up his soul upon them, using the honor as his shroud. He died at about eighty years, of such repute that he even seemed to many a sorcerer. That a learned man would never be led into the arts of sorcerers I have sufficiently said in my discourse on Dionysius; but he, I think, by his marvel-working in his themes about the ways of the Magi, drew this surname from them. They slander him too as shameless in character; for one of his pupils sent him fishes laid out on a silver dish embossed with gold, and he, overjoyed at the dish, neither gave it back nor answered the sender, "Well done, that you sent the fishes too." But this is said to have been done by way of pastime, in jest to one of his own pupils, whom he heard was using his wealth meanly; and he gave back the silver, having corrected the hearer by the witticism.

This sophist was copious in conceptions and brilliant, and most varied in the arrangements of his themes, which he had taken from tragedy, yet not orderly, nor following art; and the equipment of his diction he threw about himself from the ancient sophists, attaining rather to resonance than to ring. In many places he fell out of his grand voice, using tragedy without restraint.

Hippias the sophist of Elis had so strong a memory even in old age that, after hearing fifty names once, he could repeat them in the order in which he had heard them; and he introduced into his discourses geometry, astronomy, music, rhythms, and discoursed too about painting and sculpture. These things he did elsewhere, but at Lacedaemon he set forth the origins of cities and colonies and exploits, since the Lacedaemonians, because of their desire for empire, took pleasure in this kind of subject. There is also by him a Trojan dialogue — not a speech: in it Nestor, at the capture of Troy, suggests to Neoptolemus son of Achilles what pursuits a man should follow in order to show himself good. He went on more embassies than any of the Greeks on behalf of Elis, and nowhere did he diminish his own reputation either as a public speaker or as a converser; and he gathered very much money and was enrolled in the tribes of cities both small and great. He came also to Inycus to gather money — and this little town belongs to those Sicilians whom Plato mocks. While he was in high repute, throughout the rest of his time he charmed Greece at Olympia with elaborate and well-considered speeches. He expounded his thoughts not deficiently, but with abundance and according to nature, taking refuge in but few of the words drawn from poetry.

Greece wrongs Chrestus, the Byzantine sophist, in neglecting a man who was the best educated of the Greeks by Herodes, and educated many marvellous men, among whom were Hippodromus the sophist and Philiscus and Isagoras the tragic poet, and the renowned orators Nicomedes from Pergamon and Aquila from the eastern Galatia and Aristaenetus the Byzantine, and of those who philosophized renownedly Callaeschrus the Athenian and Sospis of the Altar and many others worthy of mention. When he was teaching, in the time of Adrianus the sophist, he had a hundred paying hearers, and the best of these were those I named. When Adrianus was established at Rome, the Athenians voted to send an embassy on behalf of Chrestus, asking the emperor for the chair at Athens for him; but he, coming forward into their assembly, dissolved the embassy, discoursing on other notable matters and saying upon all this, "The ten thousand do not make the man."

Though overcome by wine, he mastered the drunken violence and easiness and arrogance which wine brings upon the minds of men, and he had so much soberness left over that even when the drinking had advanced to cock-crow he laid hold of study before snatching sleep. He was especially at odds with the boastful among the young, although they were more useful than the rest for the contributions of the fee. At any rate, seeing Diogenes the Amastrian puffed up from boyhood, and dreaming of satrapies and of courts and of standing near kings, and saying that some Egyptian had foretold him these things, he... not even keeping silent about his own affairs.

The style of his speeches is varied from the advantages of Herodes, but falls short of their readiness, as in painting the colorless imitation sketched in shadow; and it would have advanced even to an equality of excellence, had he not died at fifty.

The name of Prodicus of Ceos became so great for wisdom that even the son of Gryllus, when he was imprisoned among the Boeotians, listened to his discourse, providing a surety for his person. When he was on an embassy to the Athenians and came forward into the council chamber, he was thought the most capable of men, although he had a voice hard to hear and heavy. He used to hunt out the young men of noble birth and from wealthy households, so that he even had agents to procure him this kind of game; for he was a slave to money and had given himself over to pleasures. The Choice of Heracles — that speech of Prodicus which I mentioned at the beginning — even Xenophon did not think it unworthy to expound. And why should I attempt to characterize the style of Prodicus, when Xenophon has sufficiently sketched it?

As for Polydeuces of Naucratis, I do not know whether one should call him uneducated or educated, or, what will seem foolish, both uneducated and educated; for when I consider his vocabulary, he had sufficiently exercised his tongue in Atticizing diction, but when I look at the form of his declamations, he Atticized no better than another.

The following, then, must be known about him. Polydeuces had sufficiently practised criticism, having kept company with his father, who knew critical discourse; but the sophistical kinds of speech he attempted with boldness rather than art, trusting his nature, for indeed he was excellently gifted by nature. Having been a pupil of Adrianus, he stands equally distant from his advantages and his deficiencies, for he least falls and least rises; but nonetheless there are certain drops of pleasure mingled into his speech. The style of his discourse was thus: "Proteus of Pharos, the Homeric marvel — many and manifold are his shapes, for he is raised into water and is kindled into fire and rages into a lion and rushes as a boar and moves as a serpent and leaps as a leopard, and if he becomes a tree, he grows leaves." And let us make a character of his declamation by the islanders who sell their families for the payment of the tribute, since they wish this theme to be best spoken too, the conclusion of which is thus: "A boy of the mainland, from Babylon, writes to his island father: I am a slave to the king, given as a gift by a satrap, and I neither mount a Median horse nor take a Persian bow, nor do I go out to war or the hunt as a man, but I sit in the women's quarters and serve the king's concubines, and the king is not angry, for I am a eunuch. And I win repute among them, describing the Greek sea and telling tales of the fair things of the Greeks: how the Eleans hold their festival, how the Delphians prophesy, what the Altar of Pity is at Athens. But you too, father, write me when the Hyacinthia is among the Lacedaemonians, and the Isthmia among the Corinthians, and the Pythia among the Delphians, and whether the Athenians are victorious in the sea-fight. Farewell, and greet my brother for me, if he has not yet been sold." Such things, then, as belong to this man it is possible for those who hear impartially to consider. And by impartial hearers I mean those who are neither well-disposed nor ill-disposed. He was said to deliver these things too with a honeyed voice, by which, having charmed the emperor Commodus, he obtained from him the chair at Athens. He lived, then, fifty-eight years, and died leaving a son legitimate indeed, but uneducated.

Polus of Acragas was trained as a sophist by Gorgias for much money, so they say; for indeed Polus was one of the wealthy. There are those who say that Polus was the first to discover the balanced clauses and the antitheses and the like endings, but they are not right; for that brilliance of speech, once discovered, Polus merely used to excess, on which account Plato, spitting him out for this ambition, says, "Best of men, Polus — to address you in your own manner."

Caesarea of the Cappadocians, neighbor to Mount Argaeus, is the home of Pausanias the sophist. Pausanias was educated by Herodes and became one of those who shared the Clepsydrium, whom the many called "the thirsty"; and he reproduced many of the advantages of Herodes, especially the improvising, but he delivered them with a thick tongue, and as is customary with the Cappadocians, clashing together the consonants of his letters, shortening what should be long and lengthening what is short, on which account the many called him a cook seasoning costly dishes badly. The style of his declamation is rather supine, yet nonetheless vigorous, and it does not miss the ancient, as one may gather from his declamations, for there are many of Pausanias' at Rome, where indeed he lived out his life and died already growing old, sharing in the chair there; and he shared too in that at Athens, when indeed, departing thence, upon all that he went through to the Athenians, he most fittingly uttered the line of Euripides: "Theseus, turn me back again, that I may see the city."

Those who write Thrasymachus of Chalcedon also among the sophists seem to me to misunderstand Plato, that to shave a lion and to play the false accuser of Thrasymachus are one and the same thing; for that passage occurs where Plato charges him with composing speeches for the courts and with wearing himself out as a false accuser in the law courts.

Athenodorus the sophist, in what pertains to his father, was the most distinguished of the men of Aenus, but in what pertains to his teachers and education, the most conspicuous of the Greek world. For he heard Aristocles while still a boy, and Chrestus when he had now come to understanding, on which account he was blended from both, Atticizing and expounding with amplitude. Teaching at Athens at the time when Polydeuces also taught, he mocked him in his discourses as boyish, saying, "The gardens of Tantalus seem to me the lightness and superficiality of his speech," likening it to an appearance that both is and is not. And being weighty also in character, he died still in his prime, robbed by Fortune of advancing even further in reputation.

As for Antiphon of Rhamnus, I do not know whether one ought to call him good or base. Let him be called good for the following reasons: he held many commands, he won many victories, he increased the navy of the Athenians by sixty fully manned triremes, and he was thought the most capable of men both to speak and to judge; for these reasons he is to be praised both by me and by another. But he might reasonably appear base for the following: he overthrew the democracy, he enslaved the people of the Athenians, he favored Sparta, at first secretly, later openly, and he loosed upon the affairs of the Athenians the tyranny of the Four Hundred.

Brilliantly among the sophists did Ptolemy of Naucratis too resound. For he was one of those who shared the temple about Naucratis, a privilege belonging to few of the Naucratites; and he was a hearer of Herodes, but not, however, an emulator, but was rather carried toward Polemo, for the rush of his speech and the breath and the speaking with amplitude he introduced from the stage of Polemo, and he is said to have improvised too with an irresistible fluency. He nibbled at suits and law courts, yet not so as to raise a name from there. They surnamed him "Marathon," as some say, since he was enrolled in the deme of Marathon at Athens, but as I heard from some, since in the Attic themes he often made mention of those who took the lead in the danger at Marathon.

As for rhetoric, some say that Antiphon discovered it when it did not yet exist, others that he developed it after it had been discovered; and as to his becoming wise, some say he was self-taught, others that he had it from his father. For they say that his father was Sophilus, a teacher of rhetorical discourse, who instructed both other men of influence and the son of Cleinias. Antiphon became most persuasive, and was surnamed Nestor for the saying that he could persuade men of anything; and he advertised consolatory lectures, on the ground that there was no grief so terrible that he could not banish it from the mind. Comedy attacks Antiphon as a man clever in matters of the courts, who sold for much money speeches composed against justice, and chiefly to those very men who were in danger. What sort of thing this is, I will make plain. Men, in the other sciences and arts, honor those who excel in each, and admire physicians who are abler over those who are less so, and admire in divination and music the more skilled, casting the same vote about carpentry and all the manual crafts; but rhetoric they praise, yet suspect as a thing cunning and money-loving and composed against justice. And it is not the many who hold this view of the art rather than the most distinguished even of serious men; at any rate they call "clever orators" those who understand well and expound well, giving no auspicious name to this advantage. And since the matter has such a nature, it was not unlikely, I think, that Antiphon too should become a subject of comedy, since comedy most of all makes comedy of things worthy of speech.

Some accuse Ptolemy of not discerning the themes, nor where they hold together and where not, setting forth as proof of this accusation the following. The Thebans indict the Messenians for "ingratitude," because they did not receive their fugitives when Thebes too was captured by Alexander. For this theme, brilliantly and as wisely as possible argued by him, they bring a false charge, saying that if they are tried while Alexander lives, who is so bold as to condemn the Messenians? But if while he is dead, who is so gentle as to acquit them of the charge? For those who slander these things do not understand that the defense of the Messenians stands upon pardon, holding before them Alexander and the fear of him, of which not even the rest of Greece was inexperienced. Let this be my defense on behalf of the man, deprecating for him an unjust and knavishly contrived charge; for indeed he was the most auspicious of the sophists. And though he visited very many nations and consorted with very many cities, nowhere did he slander his own renown, nor did he seem inferior to what was expected, but as though travelling on a brilliant chariot of fame he passed through the cities. He died, an old man, in Egypt, not deprived of his eyes by the flow from his head, but with their vision dimmed.

He died, then, in Sicily at the hands of Dionysius the tyrant; but the reasons for which he died we ascribe to Antiphon rather than to Dionysius. For he used to disparage the tragedies of Dionysius, on which Dionysius prided himself more than on being a tyrant; and when the tyrant was busying himself about the excellence of bronze, and asked those present what continent or island produces the best bronze, Antiphon, happening to be by, said, "I know the best — that at Athens, of which the statues of Harmodius and Aristogeiton are made." For this he died, as one creeping up against Dionysius and turning the Sicilians against him. But Antiphon erred, first, in offending a tyrant under whom he had chosen to live rather than be a democrat at home; next, in freeing the Sicilians while enslaving the Athenians. Moreover, in drawing Dionysius away from writing tragedy, he was drawing him away from idleness; for such pursuits are idle pursuits, and tyrants are more to be desired by their subjects when relaxed than when strained, for if they relax they will kill less, plunder and seize less; whereas a tyrant who applies himself to tragedies should be likened to a physician who is sick but is treating himself. For the making of fables, the monodies, the rhythms of the choruses, and the imitation of characters, of which the greater part must appear good, transform tyrants from what is inexorable and violent, just as draughts of medicine transform diseases. Let us consider this not an accusation of Antiphon, but advice to all, not to provoke tyrannies, nor to drive savage characters to anger.

Of his forensic speeches there are several, in which the formidable cleverness and all that comes from art are contained; and there are also others that are sophistical, but the most sophistical is the speech On Concord, in which there are brilliant and philosophical maxims, a dignified delivery adorned with poetic words, and the passages expounded at length resemble smooth plains.

As for Critias the sophist, if he overthrew the people of the Athenians, he is not yet base for that — for such a people might well be overthrown even by itself, being so puffed up as not to listen even to its lawful magistrates. But since he openly favored Sparta, betrayed the temples, demolished the walls through Lysander, and deprived of any standing-place in Greece those Athenians whom he was driving out, by proclaiming a Laconian war against all who should receive a fugitive Athenian; and since in cruelty and bloodthirstiness he surpassed the Thirty, and joined the Lacedaemonians in their monstrous design that Attica might be declared a pasture for sheep, emptied of its herd of men — for these reasons he appears to me the basest of all men who have a name for baseness.

Euodianus of Smyrna traced his descent to Nicetes the sophist, and his honors at home to the high priests and those crowned with the office over the arms, and his prizes for his voice to Rome and the chair there. Being appointed also over the artists about Dionysus — and this tribe is haughty and hard to govern — he seemed most suited to the office and above incurring blame. When his son died at Rome he uttered nothing womanish or ignoble, but calling out "O child" three times he buried him. As he was dying at Rome all his friends were present, and as they deliberated about his body, whether they should bury it on the spot or embalm it and convey it to Smyrna, Euodianus cried out, "I will not leave my son alone." So wisely did he enjoin being buried with his child. Having been a hearer of Aristocles, he laid hold of the panegyrical style, blending in a harsh mixing-bowl a kind of sweet draught. And there are those who say that he heard Polemo too.

And if it was as an uneducated man that he was led into these deeds, the argument would hold good for those who say that he was corrupted by Thessaly and his associations there; for uneducated characters are altogether easily led astray in their choice of life. But since he was most excellently educated, and expounded many maxims, and traced his descent to Dropides, who ruled the Athenians after Solon, he would not escape, in the eyes of the multitude, the charge that it was not without baseness of nature that he erred in these things. For indeed this too is strange — that he was not made like Socrates son of Sophroniscus, with whom he philosophized most of all, a man held to be the wisest and most just of his time, but was made like the Thessalians, among whom arrogance and unmixed wine and tyrannical schemes over the cup are the serious business. And yet not even the Thessalians neglected wisdom, but small and greater cities in Thessaly "Gorgianized," looking to Gorgias of Leontini; and they would have changed to "Critianizing" too, if Critias had made any display of his own wisdom among them. But he neglected this, and made their oligarchies more grievous to them by conversing with the powerful men there, and by attacking all democracy and slandering the Athenians as the people that erred most of all men; so that, when one considers this, Critias would seem to have corrupted the Thessalians rather than the Thessalians Critias.

He died, then, at the hands of the followers of Thrasybulus, who were bringing the people back from exile; and to some he seems to have proved a good man at the end, since he made the tyranny his shroud. But for my part let it be declared that no man dies nobly for the things he has wrongly chosen; on which account it seems to me that both the wisdom of the man and his studied works have been the less esteemed by the Greeks. For if speech does not agree with character, we shall seem to be sounding with another's tongue, like flutes.

As for the style of his speech, Critias was dogmatic and rich in maxims, and most capable of dignified expression — not the dithyrambic kind of dignity, nor one that takes refuge in words drawn from poetry, but composed of the most proper words and according to nature. I see the man both abridging his words sufficiently, and attacking forcefully in the manner of a defense, and using the Attic dialect not immoderately nor strangely — for tastelessness in Atticizing is barbarous — but, like the gleams of sunbeams, the Attic words shine through his speech. And to fall upon a passage without connectives is the prime of Critias, and to conceive paradoxically and to deliver paradoxically is the contest of Critias; but the breath of his speech is somewhat deficient, yet sweet and smooth, like the breeze of the West Wind.

The Siren that stands over the tomb of Isocrates the sophist — and it stands as though singing — denounces the persuasiveness of the man, which he contributed to the rules and habits of rhetoric, since he was not the first to discover the balanced clauses and antitheses and like endings, but used well what had been discovered; and he took care also for amplitude and rhythm and arrangement and resonance. These things, I dare say, prepared the way also for the tongue of Demosthenes; for Demosthenes, who was a pupil of Isaeus but an emulator of Isocrates, surpassed him in spirit and impetus and amplitude and swiftness both of speech and of thought. But the dignity of Demosthenes is rather strained and intent, while that of Isocrates is more delicate and sweeter. Let us take an example of the dignity of Demosthenes: "Death is the end of life for all men, even if a man should keep himself shut up and guarded in a little chamber; but good men must always set their hands to all that is noble, putting forward good hope, and must bear nobly whatever the god may give." And the dignity of Isocrates is adorned thus: "Seeing that the whole earth that lies beneath the heaven has been cut in two, and the one part is called Asia, the other Europe, the King has taken the half of it by the treaties, as though dividing the territory against Zeus himself."

As for Rufus of Perinthus the sophist, let it not be from his estate, nor that many consuls were his line, nor that he held with glory the office of the Panhellenia at Athens — for these things, even if much were said of them, are not yet worthy to be set beside the man's wisdom — but let his tongue make him plain, and the understanding which he used most of all about the figured themes. In this style he was admired, first, because it is hard to interpret, for in themes composed by figure one needs a rein for what is said and a sting for what is kept silent, and next, I think, because of his own nature; for being open in character and without knavery, he played well even what was not in his nature. Being the richest of those about the Hellespont and the Propontis, and having much reputation for improvising, much both at Athens and in Ionia and Italy, he nowhere brought himself into enmity with either a city or a man, but was a dealer in gentleness. He was said too to strengthen his body with gymnastic, eating by rule always and toiling at it like those who contend in the games. Having been a hearer of Herodes among boys and of Aristocles among youths, and deemed worthy of great things by him, he made himself brilliant rather to Herodes, calling him his master and the tongue of the Greeks and the king of speeches and many such things. He died at home, sixty-one years old, and leaving children, about whom I have nothing great to say, except indeed that they were his.

He shrank from politics and kept away from the assemblies, both because of the deficiency of his voice and because of the envy at Athens which works in opposition above all against those who speak more wisely than the rest. Yet he did not give up concern for public affairs; for both in what he wrote to Philip he was setting matters right, no doubt, on behalf of the Athenians, and in what he composed about the peace he was diverting the Athenians from the sea, on the ground that they bore an ill name upon it; and there is by him a Panegyric oration, which he delivered at Olympia, persuading Greece to march against Asia and to cease from their domestic quarrels.

This man, then, though his speeches are most beautiful, nonetheless gave occasion for the charge that the Panegyric was put together out of what Gorgias had worked up on the same theme. The best composed of Isocrates' studied works are the Archidamus and the speech Without Witnesses; for through the former there runs a high spirit, recalling the events at Leuctra, and not only are the words precise, but the arrangement too is brilliant, and the speech is full of contest, so that even its mythical part, that about Heracles and the cattle, is expounded with vigor; while the Without Witnesses displays a force chastened to rhythms, for thought ends from thought in periods of equal members.

The pupils of this man were many, but the most distinguished was Hyperides the orator; for Theopompus of Chios and Ephorus of Cyme I would neither disparage nor admire. Those who think that comedy attacks the man as a flute-maker are mistaken; for his father was Theodorus, whom they called a flute-maker at Athens, but he himself knew nothing about flutes nor any other of the manual crafts, since he would not even have obtained his statue at Olympia if he had worked at anything mean. He died, then, at Athens at about a hundred years; and let us consider him one of those who died in war, since he came to his end after Chaeronea, not enduring to hear the report of the Athenian disaster.

Concerning Aeschines son of Atrometus, whom we say to have been the founder of the second sophistic, the following must be considered. The popular leadership at Athens was wholly divided, and some were friendly to the King, others to the Macedonians; and the foremost of those who favored the King was Demosthenes of Paeania, while of those who looked to Philip it was Aeschines of Cothocidae; and money came to them from both sides, the King keeping Philip occupied through the Athenians so that he should not march against Asia, and Philip trying to break up the strength of the Athenians as a hindrance to his crossing. The quarrel between Aeschines and Demosthenes began both from this very thing — that each pursued his policy for a different king — and, as it seems to me, from their being opposite also in character; for from characters opposed to one another there grows a hatred that has no cause. And they were opposed for these reasons too: Aeschines was thought a lover of wine and pleasant and easygoing, and to have taken all his charm from Dionysus — for indeed in his youth he had played supporting parts in tragedy to the deep-toned actors — while Demosthenes appeared clouded over and heavy of brow and a drinker of water, on which account he was set down among the morose and ill-tempered, and much the more so since, when the two were on an embassy with others to Philip and lived together, the one appeared expansive and pleasant to his fellow ambassadors, the other reserved and always in earnest. Their quarrel was intensified by the speech about Amphipolis before Philip, when Demosthenes broke down in his speech, while Aeschines was not even among those who had ever thrown away their shields — as one may consider by recalling the action at Tamynae, in which the Athenians defeated the Boeotians. For this he was publicly crowned with the prize of valor, among other things for having used incredible speed in carrying the good tidings of the victory.

Onomarchus the sophist from Andros was not admired, but appeared not to be blamed. For he taught at the time when Adrianus and Chrestus did at Athens, and being a neighbor of Asia he drew, like an eye-disease, the Ionic style, which was especially cultivated at Ephesus, on which account some thought he had not even heard Herodes, slandering the man; for in his expression he was corrupted in some places for the reason I have said, but the casts of his thoughts were Herodean and ineffably sweet. One may consider him from the lover of the statue, if I shall not seem to play the boy. It is said thus: "O living beauty in a soulless body, what divinity then fashioned you? Some Persuasion, or Grace, or Eros himself, the father of beauty? How everything is present to you in truth — the set of the face, the bloom of color, the sting of the glance, the gracious smile, the blush of the cheeks, the trace of hearing. And you have too a voice ever about to speak. Perhaps you even say something, but when I am not present, you loveless and grudging thing, faithless to a faithful lover. You shared with me no word; therefore I will lay upon you the most dreadful curse of all that is ever set upon the beautiful: I pray you to grow old." Of his death some say it was at Athens, others at home, half-grey and passing into old age; and that he became rather rustic in appearance and after the manner of Marcus the Byzantine's squalor.

When Demosthenes accused him of being responsible for the Phocian disaster, the Athenians acquitted him of the charge; but on the condemnation of Antiphon he was caught without trial, and the members of the Areopagus deprived him of the right to plead for them concerning the temple at Delos. And further, although he had been proclaimed a delegate to the Amphictyonic council, he has not even yet escaped, in the eyes of the multitude, the charge that it was he who set Philip over Elatea, after throwing the council of the Amphictyons into confusion with specious speeches and fables. He withdrew from Athens, not having been commanded to go into exile, but removing himself because of the loss of civic rights to which he was being subjected by Demosthenes and Ctesiphon, having been defeated in the voting. His first impulse in going abroad was toward Alexander, on the supposition that he would presently come to Babylon and Susa; but having put in at Ephesus, and hearing both that Alexander was dead and that the affairs of Asia were so confounded, he held to Rhodes; and the island is a good one to study in, and, having made Rhodes a thinking-place of sophists, he passed his life there, sacrificing to quiet and the Muses, and mingling Attic with Dorian ways.

As for the extempore speech, delivered with fluency and divine inspiration, he was the first to win this praise. For speaking divinely had not yet become customary in the studies of the sophists, but it began with Aeschines, who improvised with god-possessed impulse, like those who breathe forth oracles. Having been a pupil of Plato and Isocrates, he drew much also from his own nature. For there is in his speech the light of clarity, and a delicate dignity, and charm joined with formidable power; and altogether the style of his speech is too great to be brought under imitation.

Of the speeches of Aeschines there is, according to some, even a fourth, a Deliac oration, which falsely claims his tongue. For he would never have arranged the speeches about Amphissa, by which the Cirrhaean land was made sacred, with such fair show and grace while plotting evil for the Athenians, as Demosthenes says, and yet have set out so feebly upon the Deliac myths, in which there is theology and theogony and antiquarian lore — and this when contending on behalf of the Athenians, who considered it no small contest not to be cast out of the temple at Delos. Let the tongue of Aeschines, then, be bounded by three speeches: the one Against Timarchus, the defense On the Embassy, and the prosecution of Ctesiphon. There is also a fourth studied work of his: letters, not many, but full of good education and character.

Of his moral quality he gave a display to the Rhodians too; for when he once read in public the speech Against Ctesiphon, and some wondered how he had been defeated with such a speech, and reproached the Athenians as out of their minds, he said, "You would not wonder if you had heard Demosthenes speaking against it" — thereby not only setting himself to praise his enemy, but also acquitting the jurors of blame.

Passing over Ariobarzanes the Cilician and Xenophron the Sicilian and Pithagoras of Cyrene, who were thought neither capable of understanding nor of expounding what they understood, but were valued by the Greeks of their own time for lack of noble sophists — much as bitter vetch is valued by those who are short of grain — let us go on to Nicetes of Smyrna. For this Nicetes, taking over the science when it had been confined within narrow bounds, gave it approaches far more splendid than those he himself built for Smyrna, joining the city to the gates leading to Ephesus, and, by their grandeur, raising up deeds to match his words. This man was thought better in forensic matters by the men of the courts, and better in sophistical matters by the sophists, because he had ambidextrously and emulously fashioned himself for both. For he adorned the forensic with sophistical amplitude, and strengthened the sophistical with a forensic sting. The style of his speeches has departed from the ancient and political; it is somewhat Bacchic and dithyrambic, and gives forth its conceptions, peculiar and paradoxical, as the Bacchic thyrsus gives forth honey and the swarms of milk.

Apollonius of Naucratis taught in opposition to Heracleides, who had seized the chair at Athens, and he cultivated a speech political and well-chastened, but contending less, for amplitude is absent from him, and breath. As he was bad in matters of love, there was born to him a son from an unlawful marriage, Rufinus, who played the sophist after him with nothing fertile, nor from the heart, but holding to his father's little phrases and trifling thoughts; on which account he too, being charged by a wise man, said, "The laws give me leave to use my father's possessions," and the other said, "They give leave, but to those born according to law." Some attack him too for going to Macedonia hired by a house that was not even prospering. But let such things be dismissed; for you would find even some of the very wise doing many illiberal things for money, yet not this Apollonius, for he both made his estate common to the Greeks who were in need, and was not severe about agreeing on a fee. He died at seventy at Athens, having as his shroud the goodwill of all the Athenians. He was a hearer of the sophists Adrianus and Chrestus, but stands as far from both as those who never heard them. He surveyed his themes withdrawing from the crowd, but for more time than was moderate.

Although he was held worthy of great honors — for what did not Smyrna cry out about him, as about a marvellous man and orator? — he did not often go before the people, but, being charged by the multitude with timidity, he said, "I am more afraid of a people when it exalts than when it reviles." Once when a tax-collector grew insolent toward him in a law court and said, "Stop barking at me," Nicetes very wittily replied, "By Zeus, I will — if you too stop biting me." His journey beyond the Alps and the Rhine came about by an imperial command, and the cause of it was this. A man of consular rank, whose name was Rufus, was auditing the accounts of the Smyrnaeans bitterly and harshly. Having offended him in some way, Nicetes said, "Farewell," and no longer came before him as he sat in judgment. Now, during the time when Rufus governed but a single city, he did not yet think he had been grievously treated; but when he was entrusted with the Celtic legions, he remembered his anger — for prosperity, among its other effects, makes men no longer able to endure the things they had endured, by human reckoning, before they fared well — and he wrote to the emperor Nerva many bitter complaints against Nicetes. And the emperor himself said, "Give him a hearing while he makes his defense, and if you find him guilty, impose the penalty." This he wrote not to give Nicetes up, but to prepare Rufus for pardon; for never would Rufus, against a man who had thus been put in his power, either put him to death or punish anyone else, lest he should appear oppressive to the man who had appointed him judge of his enemy. For these reasons, then, he went to the Rhine and the Celts, and, coming forward to make his defense, he so struck Rufus with awe that Rufus shed more tears over Nicetes than the water that had been measured out to him, and sent him away not only unwounded but the object of all eyes and among the envied of the Smyrnaeans. This man, some time later, Heracleides the Lycian sophist undertook to correct, and entitled him "Nicetes the Purged"; but he did not perceive that he was fitting Pygmy first-fruits to a colossus.

Isaeus the sophist, the Assyrian, in his youth had given himself to pleasures; for he was a slave to gluttony and hard drinking, wore fine clothes, was often in love, and revelled without concealment; but when he came to manhood he so changed that he was thought a different man from a different man. For he took away from his face and mind the love of laughter that seemed to float upon him; he no longer attended even on the stage the strains of lyres and flutes; he put off his mantles and the dyed colors of his cloaks, restrained his table, and laid aside his loves, as though he had thrown away his former eyes. At any rate, when Ardys the orator asked him whether such-and-such a woman seemed fair to him, Isaeus replied most temperately, "I have ceased to suffer from eye-trouble." And when another asked him which is the best of birds and fishes for eating, Isaeus said, "I have ceased to take such things seriously, for I have come to understand that I was gleaning the gardens of Tantalus" — indicating, no doubt, to his questioner, that all pleasures are shadows and dreams.

Apollonius the Athenian was deemed worthy of a name among the Greeks, as capable in forensic matters and not to be blamed in declamation; and he taught at Athens, in the time of Heracleides and his namesake, presiding over the political chair for a talent. Becoming conspicuous in political matters too, he both went on embassies on the greatest affairs and was entrusted with the public services which the Athenians consider greatest, the eponymous office and that over the arms, and he was entrusted with the utterances from the shrine when already growing old, falling short of Heracleides and Logimus and Glaucus and such hierophants in good voice, but in dignity and magnificence and orderliness seeming to surpass many of those above.

When Dionysius of Miletus, who was his pupil, used to make his declamations with a kind of chanting, Isaeus rebuked him, saying, "Young man of Ionia, I did not teach you to sing." And when a young Ionian expressed admiration to him for the saying of Nicetes, grandly uttered concerning Xerxes, "Let us moor Aegina to the royal ship," Isaeus laughed broadly and said, "Foolish fellow, and how will you put to sea?" He made his declamations not extempore, but considered through the hours from dawn to midday. He cultivated a style of speech neither overlaid nor dry, but unencumbered and according to nature and sufficient to the matters in hand. The expounding of things briefly, both this and the compressing of an entire theme into a brief compass, was the invention of Isaeus, as was shown in many other instances, but most of all in these. For when he was arguing the case of the Lacedaemonians who were deliberating about the wall, he made his point briefly from the words of Homer to this effect: "Shield pressed on shield, helmet on helmet, man on man; thus stand for me, Lacedaemonians, and we are walled." And when he was prosecuting Python of Byzantium, on the ground that he had been imprisoned by oracle on a charge of treason, and the treason had been judged proven when Philip withdrew, he compressed this case into three thoughts; for what he said is contained in these three: "I prove that Python betrayed the god who gave the oracle, the people who imprisoned him, and Philip who withdrew; for the one would not have given the oracle had there been nothing in it, the other would not have imprisoned him had he not been such a man, and the third would not have withdrawn had he not failed to find the man for whose sake he had come."

Being on an embassy to Severus the emperor at Rome, he stripped for the contest over declamation against Heracleides the sophist, and the one went away deprived of his immunity, while Apollonius went away with gifts. And when Heracleides spread an untrue story about Apollonius, that he was about to go to Libya, when the emperor was there and was gathering the excellences from all the earth, and said to him, "It is time for you to read the speech against Leptines," Apollonius said, "For you, rather, since it has been written about immunity too."

The starting-line of his speech Apollonius cast from the style of Adrianus, since he was indeed his hearer, but he diverges nonetheless into measured and anapaestic rhythms, which, if he guarded against them, he seems dignified in delivery and steady. This one may find both in other themes and most of all in the Callias, who forbids the Athenians to bury with fire: "Raise high, man, the torch. Why do you force it and bring it down and torment the fire? It is heavenly, it is ethereal; the fire goes to its kindred. It does not bring down corpses, but leads up gods. Io Prometheus, torch-bearer and fire-bringer, how your gift is outraged! It is mingled with senseless corpses. Help, aid, steal, if possible, the fire even from there." I have set forth these things not to deprecate for him the undisciplined rhythms, but to teach that he was not ignorant of the more temperate rhythms either. He died, then, at about seventy-five years, copious and breathing strongly among the people of the Athenians, and he was buried in the suburb of the highroad to Eleusis. The name of the suburb is Sacred Fig Tree, and there they rest the sacred things from Eleusis whenever they bring them to the city.

I shall discourse about Scopelianus the sophist, having first attacked those who try to disparage him; for they deem the man unworthy of the circle of the sophists, calling him dithyrambic and undisciplined and coarse. Such things about him are said by the petty quibblers, the sluggish, who breathe nothing of an extempore tongue. For by nature man is an envious creature: at any rate the small disparage the tall, the ugly the handsome, the slow and lame the light and swift, the cowardly the bold, the unmusical the lyric poets, the untrained the wrestlers; and one should not wonder if certain men, hobbled in their tongue and with an ox of dumbness set upon it, men who could neither conceive anything great themselves nor assent when another conceived it, should spit upon and disparage the man who, of all the Greeks of his time, expounded most readily and boldly and grandly. How they have failed to know the man, I will make plain, and what the very fashion of his house was.

I will record too Proclus of Naucratis, knowing the man well, for indeed he was one of my own teachers. Proclus, then, was one of the not undistinguished men in Egypt, but seeing Naucratis in faction and men governing against their character, he loved the quiet at Athens and, sailing away thither secretly, he lived there, having brought much money and many slaves and the rest of his furnishings magnificently arrayed. Being of good report at Athens and having won repute in his youth, he won it much more when he became a man, first for his choice of life, and next, I think, also for a benefaction done to one Athenian, which provided a demonstration of a good character. For sailing into the Piraeus he asked one of the men there whether so-and-so was living well at Athens and faring well; and he asked this about the guest-friend with whom he had associated at Athens when young, when indeed he frequented Adrianus. And learning that he both existed and lived, but was about to be cast at once out of his house, which was being proclaimed for sale in the market-place for ten thousand drachmas, which he had borrowed upon it, he sent him the ten thousand before he had even gone up to the city, saying, "Free the house, that I may not see you downcast." Let us consider this the act not only of a rich man, but of one using his wealth well, sufficiently educated and exact in matters of friendship.

He was high priest of Asia, both he and his ancestors before him, son from father all of them; and this crown is a great one, and bestowed for much expenditure. He was born a twin: both children lay in swaddling-clothes, but when they were five days old one of them was struck by lightning, while the other was not maimed in any of his senses, though he lay beside the one who was struck. And yet the fire of thunderbolts is so keen and sulphurous that of those near it some it kills by the shock, some it injures in their hearing and eyes, some it strikes down in their wits. But Scopelianus was caught by none of these, for he continued even to deep old age unimpaired and sound. Whence I marvel at this I wish to make plain to you. Eight reapers were dining in Lemnos beneath a great oak near the place called the Horn of the island — and this place is a harbor that curves into slender points — and when a cloud enveloped the oak and a thunderbolt was discharged into it, the oak was struck, and the reapers, a panic falling upon them, died each just as he happened to be engaged: one as he was raising a cup, one as he was drinking, one as he was kneading, one as he was eating, one as he was doing something else, they gave up their souls scorched and black, like the bronze of statues smoked over the fiery springs. But Scopelianus was so reared, not without divine favor, that he escaped the death from the thunderbolt, which not even the toughest of the rustics escaped, and remained unwounded in his senses, with his mind ready and stronger than sleep; for indeed sluggishness too was absent from him.

He acquired houses too, two in the city, one in the Piraeus and another at Eleusis. There came to him from Egypt frankincense, ivory, perfume, papyrus, books, and all such merchandise, and selling these to the dealers in such things he nowhere seemed money-loving or illiberal, nor a lover of the greater, nor seeking profits or interest, but loving the principal itself. To a profligate son, who was young along with him about the rearing of cocks and quails and dogs and lapdogs and horses, more than rebuking him, and having a charge with the multitude for it, he said, "The playing with old men will sooner change than the playing with one's own age-mates." When his son died, and his wife too, he took a concubine, because even aging eyes seek the beautiful; but as she became most womanish, giving her all rein, he seemed not a good steward of his house.

He attended, for the rhetorical part of his speeches, upon Nicetes of Smyrna, who declaimed brilliantly, but breathed much more mightily in the law courts. When the Clazomenians begged him to make his declamations at home, thinking that Clazomenae would advance greatly if such a man instructed in their city, he declined it not without grace, saying that the nightingale does not sing in a little cage; and he looked upon Smyrna as a kind of grove for his own euphony, and considered the echo there to be worth most of all. For of all Ionia, settled as it is like a single museum, Smyrna holds the most perfect place, just as among instruments the bridge does.

The customary rules of declamation for this man were thus: by paying a hundred drachmas once for all, one might hear for all time. He had too a chest of books in his house, of which those gathered for the fullness of the hearing had a share. And that we might not hiss at one another, nor mock, which is wont to happen in the gatherings of the sophists, we were called in all together and sat when summoned, the boys and the tutors in the middle, the youths by themselves. To discourse rested with him on rare occasions, but whenever he set out to discourse he resembled both one driving horses and one Gorgianizing. The declamation, considered the day before, was wheeled in. His power of memory, already growing old at ninety, was strong even beyond Simonides, and he expounded according to nature, but the casts of his thoughts were Adrianic.

The reasons why his father, from being mild and gentle, became harsh toward him are told in many forms — for it was this woman and that, and several besides — but I will declare the truest. After the mother of Scopelianus, the old man took a woman to wife in a half-marriage and not according to law, and Scopelianus, seeing this, used to admonish him and try to draw him away; but this is disagreeable to men past their prime. She, in turn, composed a story against him, that he was in love with her, but could not endure her error. There joined her in these slanders a servant of the old man, a cook surnamed Cytherus, who fawned upon his master, as in a play, and said such things as these: "Master, your son wishes you already dead, not even granting your old age the natural death that will come before long, but himself working at the plot and hiring my hands too. For he has man-slaying drugs prepared against you, the most deadly of which he bids me throw into one of the dishes, promising me freedom and fields and houses and money and whatever I wish to have of your estate; and these things are mine if I obey, but if I disobey, scourging and the rack and heavy fetters and a grievous pillory." And having gone round his master with such flatteries, when the old man died not long after and was making his will, Cytherus was written down as heir, and was called his son and his eyes and his whole soul. And one need not wonder at this, since he charmed an old man in love and perhaps also wandering in his wits through age and through love itself — for indeed even young men in love, there is not one of them who keeps his own mind — but the wonder is that he was thought stronger than the formidable power of Scopelianus and his eminence in the law courts, contending against him about the will, and stretching out against that man's cleverness that man's own wealth. For by draining off the estate and hiring with excessive sums all tongues together and the votes of jurors everywhere, he carried off the victory; on which account Scopelianus used to say that the lands of Anaxagoras had become a pasture for sheep, but his own a pasture for slaves. And when Cytherus, who had become distinguished in public affairs too, was now growing old, and saw his estate dwindling, and was sufficiently despised, and even received blows from a man from whom he happened to be demanding money, he became a suppliant of Scopelianus, that he would set aside his resentment and anger, and recover the house of his father, conceding to Cytherus a portion of it, since it was large, that he might not live there in unfree fashion, and granting him two of the farms by the sea. And a part of the house in which he lived out his life is even now called "the House of Cytherus." These things I tell so that they may not be unknown, and that from them too one may understand that men are the playthings not of god alone, but also of one another.

While Scopelianus was teaching at Smyrna, there resorted to it Ionians and Lydians and Carians and Maeonians, Aeolians too and the Greeks from Mysia and the Phrygians — but this was nothing great, for Smyrna lies close at the door of these peoples, holding conveniently the gates of land and sea; yet he drew Cappadocians too and Assyrians, he drew Egyptians and Phoenicians and the more distinguished of the Achaeans and all the youth from Athens. He had, indeed, given the multitude the impression of ease and carelessness, since the time before declamation he spent for the most part with the magistrates of the Smyrnaeans over public affairs; but he drew upon a nature that was brilliant and high-minded, and he studied less in the daytime, and being a man of the least sleep he used to say, "O Night, for you indeed have the greatest share of wisdom among the gods," and he made her a fellow-worker in his studies. At any rate he is said to have prolonged his work from evening to dawn. He applied himself to all kinds of poetry, but glutted himself with tragedy, contending against the grand voice of his teacher — for it was in this respect that Nicetes was greatly admired — and he drove grandeur of voice to such a height that he even composed a Gigantia and handed to the Homerids material for their verse. Among the sophists he kept company most of all with Gorgias of Leontini, and among the orators with those who ring out brilliantly. The charm he had by nature rather than by practice, for it belongs to the nature of the Ionians to be witty, and in his speeches too the love of laughter prevailed in him, for he considered the downcast countenance to be unsociable and disagreeable. He came before the popular assemblies too with a relaxed and expansive countenance, and much the more so when they met in anger, soothing them and calming them by the cheerfulness of his look. His character in the law courts was neither money-loving nor abusive; for he arranged himself without fee on the side of those in danger of their lives, and those who railed in their speeches and thought to make some display of spirit he called drunken old women raving. He made his declamations for a fee, but the fee was different for different men and according to each man's means; and he came before them neither disdainful and pompous, nor like those who are afraid, but as it was natural for one to be who was anxious about his own reputation, yet confident that he would not stumble. He discoursed from the chair with delicacy, but when he discoursed standing his speech had vehemence and was vigorous. And he considered his themes not within, nor in the crowd, but withdrawing for a short time he surveyed everything. He had also a surplus of euphony, and his voice had a sweetness, and he often struck his thigh, rousing both himself and his hearers. He was excellent both at giving a speech a turn and at speaking on both sides; but he was more marvellous in the more vigorous themes, and much more so in the Median ones, in which the Dariuses and Xerxeses figure; for these themes he himself, it seems to me, expounded best of the sophists, and handed down to those who came after him to expound, for in them he acted out a high spirit and the levity that belongs to barbarian ways. He was said also to sway more in these, as though playing the Bacchant; and when one of Polemo's circle said that he was beating a tambourine, Scopelianus, taking up the jest, said, "I do beat a tambourine — but the shield of Ajax."

His imperial embassies were many — for indeed a kind of good fortune accompanied him when he went on an embassy — but the best was the one about the vines; for it was undertaken not on behalf of the Smyrnaeans alone, like most of them, but on behalf of all Asia together. The purport of the embassy I will make plain. It seemed good to the emperor that there should be no vines in Asia, since they were thought to fall into faction over wine, but that those already planted should be taken up, and no others planted thereafter. There was need, then, of an embassy from the commonwealth and of a man who, like an Orpheus or a Thamyris, was to charm on behalf of the vines. They all therefore choose Scopelianus; and he so prevailed in the embassy, with much to spare, that he came back not only with leave to plant, but with penalties against those who did not plant. How he won renown in the contest about the vines is shown both by what has been said — for the speech is among his most marvellous — and by what followed the speech, for he received on its account the gifts customary at the imperial court, and many greetings and praises, and a brilliant band of youth, lovers of wisdom, followed him to Ionia.

When he came to Athens, Atticus, the father of Herodes the sophist, made him his guest, admiring him for his rhetoric more than the Thessalians once admired Gorgias. At any rate, all the busts of the ancient orators that stood in the walks of his house, he ordered to be pelted with stones, as having corrupted his son. Now Herodes happened to be a youth at the time and still under his father's authority, and he was passionately fond of extempore speaking alone, yet he did not have the courage for it, for he had not yet kept company with Scopelianus up to that point of time, nor did he know what the impulse of extempore speakers was; on which account the man's visit was welcome to him. For when he heard him speaking and delivering an extempore speech, he was given wings by him and made ready, and, intending to give pleasure to his father, he reported to him a declamation in the style of their guest. His father admired him for the imitation and gave him five hundred talents; and he gave Scopelianus himself fifteen, and Herodes added to him as much again from his own gift as his father had given, calling him besides his own teacher. To one who understands Herodes, this is sweeter than even the springs of the Pactolus.

The good fortune that he enjoyed in his embassies one may gather from this too. The Smyrnaeans had need of a man to go on an embassy on their behalf, and the embassy was about the greatest matters. Scopelianus was now growing old and was past the age for travelling, and Polemo was being chosen, who had not yet been on an embassy before. So Polemo, praying for good fortune, asked that the persuasiveness of Scopelianus might become his; and embracing him before the assembly, he very wittily applied to the man the words from the Patrocleia: "Give me your armor to put about my shoulders, in case they take me for you." And Apollonius of Tyana too, who surpassed human nature in wisdom, ranks Scopelianus among the marvellous.

Whether Dionysius of Miletus, as some say, was sprung from most distinguished fathers, or, as others, from this alone — that they were free men — let that part of the matter be dismissed, since he shone by his own virtue; for to take refuge in one's forebears belongs to those who have lost the praise that is their own. Having been a pupil of Isaeus, a man who, as I have said, expounded according to nature, he sufficiently took an impression of this, and in addition the good ordering of thoughts, for this too is of Isaeus. Being most honeyed in his conceptions, he was not drunk over his pleasures, as some of the sophists are, but managed them sparingly, always saying to his intimates that one must taste honey with the fingertip and not with the hollow of the hand, as has been shown in all that Dionysius said, in logical and legal and ethical contests, but most of all in the lament over Chaeronea. For going through the part where Demosthenes, after Chaeronea, presents himself to the council, he ended this monody of his speech thus: "O Chaeronea, base spot." And again, "O Boeotia that has deserted to the barbarians. Groan, you heroes beneath the earth: near Plataea we have been defeated." And again, in the speech about the Arcadians who were on trial for serving as mercenaries: "A market of war is set before the Arcadians, and the woes of the Greeks feed Arcadia. And war comes on without a cause."

Phoenix the Thessalian is not worth admiring, nor again worth slandering in everything. For he was one of those who frequented Philagrus, better at understanding than at expounding, for what was conceived had arrangement and nothing was conceived out of season, but his expression seemed both torn apart and to stand apart from rhythm. He seemed to be more suited to those of the young who were beginning than to those who had already acquired some habit, for the matters lay bare exposed and the diction did not clothe them about. Dying at seventy at Athens, he was buried not without distinction, for he lies near those from the wars, on the right of the descent toward the Academy.

Such, on the whole, was the style of Dionysius, according to which the work of his declamation proceeded as he considered his theme for as long a time as Isaeus did. As for the story told about Dionysius — that he taught his pupils their power of memory by Chaldean arts — whence it arose, I will make plain. Arts of memory neither exist nor could exist; for memory gives the arts, but is itself untaught and captured by no art, since it is an advantage of nature or a portion of the immortal soul. For human things would never be thought mortal, nor what we have learned teachable, if memory dwelt as a fellow-citizen among men — whether one must call her the mother of time or the child, let us not quarrel with the poets, but let it be as they wish. Besides, who is so simple, when he is enrolled among the wise, as to slander his own reputation by playing the sorcerer among young men, and to slander even what he was rightly taught? Whence, then, came the power of memory to his hearers? The works of Dionysius were thought insatiable in their pleasure, and he was often compelled to repeat them, since he perceived that they delighted in the hearing. So the readier of the young men used to stamp them upon their minds and report them to others, having grasped them by practice rather than by memory, on which account they were called "men of memory" and had made it into an art. Starting from this, some say that the declamations of Dionysius were "patched together from gleanings," as though one man contributed one thing to them and another another, wherever he had spoken briefly.

Great honors, then, were paid him both from the cities, all that admired him for his wisdom, and the greatest from the emperor; for Hadrian appointed him satrap of peoples not undistinguished, and enrolled him among those who ride at public expense and those who are fed in the Museum — and the Museum is an Egyptian table that calls together the distinguished men from all over the earth. Though he visited very many cities and consorted with very many peoples, he never incurred a charge of amorousness or of imposture, by reason of his appearing most temperate and self-controlled. As for those who attribute to Dionysius the Araspas who loved Panthea, they have never heard the rhythms of Dionysius, nor the rest of his manner of expression, and are without experience of the art of his thoughts; for this work is not of Dionysius, but of Celer the rhetorical writer; and Celer was a good director of the imperial correspondence, but not adequate in declamation, and at variance with Dionysius from the time of their youth.

Nor let those things be omitted by me, who heard them from Aristaeus, the oldest of the Greeks of my time and one who knew very much about the sophists. Dionysius was growing old in brilliant repute, and Polemo was coming into his prime, not yet known to Dionysius, and was staying at Sardis, pleading a case before the Hundred Men, by whom Lydia was governed. So when Dionysius came in the evening to Sardis, he asked Dorion the critic, his guest-friend, "Tell me, Dorion, what is Polemo doing here?" And Dorion said, "A man, the richest in Lydia, in danger of losing his estate, brings Polemo from Smyrna as his advocate, having persuaded him with a fee of two talents, and he will plead the case tomorrow." And Dionysius said, "What a windfall you have told me of, if it shall be mine to hear Polemo, when I have not yet come to a trial of him." "It seems," said Dorion, "that the young man, now advancing to a great name, perplexes you." "And by Athena," said Dionysius, "he does not let me sleep, but sets my heart to leaping and my mind, when I consider how many are his praisers, and how to some his mouth seems a fountain of twelve spouts, while others measure his tongue by the cubit, like the risings of the Nile. So heal me of this anxiety by telling me what more, and what less, you have observed in me and in him." And Dorion very temperately said, "You yourself, Dionysius, will judge better between yourself and him, for you, by your wisdom, are able both to know yourself and not to be ignorant of another." Dionysius heard him plead the case, and as he was leaving the court he said, "The athlete has strength, but not from the wrestling school." When Polemo heard this, he came to the doors of Dionysius announcing a declamation to him; and when Dionysius came, and Polemo pleaded brilliantly, he came up to Dionysius and, pressing his shoulder against his, as those do who lock together in the upright wrestling of the stadium, he very wittily jeered, saying, "There were once, there were once, brave men of Miletus." Now, while of distinguished men every land is the tomb, Dionysius has a monument in most distinguished Ephesus; for he is buried in the market-place at the most central spot of Ephesus, where he ended his life after teaching the first part of his life at Lesbos.

Lollianus of Ephesus was the first to preside over the chair at Athens, and he presided also over the people of the Athenians, having held for them the office of general over the arms; and this office of old used to enroll and lead men out to war, but now it has charge of provisions and the grain-market. When a tumult arose at the bakers' shops and the Athenians had set out to stone him, Pancrates the Cynic, who afterward philosophized at the Isthmus, came forward to the Athenians and said, "Lollianus is no seller of bread, but a seller of words," and so diverted the Athenians that they let fall the stones that were in their hands. When grain had been shipped in from Thessaly and there was no public money, Lollianus authorized a contribution among his own pupils, and considerable money was collected. And this will be thought the mark of a resourceful man, wise in public affairs; but the following of a just and fair-minded one: for he gave this money back to those who had contributed it, remitting the fee for his lectures.

My account leads me to a most renowned man, Damianus from Ephesus, from whom let Soteri and Sosi and Nicandri and Phaedri and Cyri and Phylaces be excluded, for these would rather be called the playthings of the Greeks than sophists worthy of mention. Now for Damianus most renowned was both his upper lineage and men of the greatest worth to Ephesus, and most of good repute too were those born from him, for they are all deemed worthy of the senate, admired for their good repute and their disdain of money; and he himself, equipped with varied and abundant wealth, both relieved those of the Ephesians in need, and benefited the community most of all, both giving money and restoring the public works that had fallen into decay.

This sophist was thought most skilled in art and most prudent, and to have worked out adequately the technique of argumentation, which lies in artful invention; and he was sufficient in exposition, but not over-elaborate in conceiving and in arranging what he had conceived. There shine through his speech also brilliancies that quickly fade, like the flash of lightning. This is shown in all his speeches, but most of all in these. For when he was accusing Leptines on account of his law, since grain was no longer coming to the Athenians from the Pontus, he reached his height thus: "The mouth of the Pontus has been closed by a law, and a few syllables hinder the sustenance of the Athenians; and Lysander fighting at sea and Leptines fighting with a law have the same effect." And when he was opposing the Athenians, who in lack of money were planning to sell the islands, he breathed thus: "Loose, O Poseidon, the favor done to Delos; allow her, when she is sold, to flee." He improvised in the manner of Isaeus, whom indeed he had heard; and he charged generous fees, providing meetings that were not only for declamation but also for instruction. There are statues of him at Athens, one in the market-place, and another in the little grove, which he himself is said to have planted.

He joined the temple too to Ephesus, extending to it the descent through the Magnesian gate. And this is a colonnade of stone, the whole a stade long, and the purpose of the building is that the worshippers might not be away from the temple when it rains. This work, then, completed from much money, he inscribed in the name of his wife, but the banqueting hall in the temple he himself dedicated, raising it in size above all together that are among others and clothing it in a beauty beyond speech, for it is adorned with Phrygian stone, of a kind that has not yet been cut. He began to use his wealth well from boyhood; for when Aristides and Adrianus held, the one Smyrna, the other Ephesus, he heard both for ten thousand, saying that it was far sweeter to spend on such favorites than on fair men and fair women, as some do. And whatever I have recorded about these men I have said having learned it from Damianus, who knew the affairs of both well.

A demonstration of the man's wealth lay in these things too: first, the whole land, as much as he possessed, was planted with trees fruitful and well-shading, and in his estates by the sea there were islands made by hand and embankments of harbors securing the anchorages for merchant ships putting in and setting out; and houses in the suburbs, some furnished in the city manner, some cavernous; and next, the very character of the man in the market-place, who did not welcome every gain, nor praise taking from everyone, but to those whom he perceived to be in want he gave his own voice free. And it was much the same in his sophistical discourses too; for those whom he perceived to be in want, coming from nations beyond the borders, he remitted the fee for the hearing, that they might not be detected in their expense.

He was more sophistical than the forensic speaker, and more forensic than the sophist. Advancing into old age he gave up both pursuits, broken in body rather than in mind; at any rate, providing himself to those who came to Ephesus on his fame, he devoted to me too a certain companionship, first and second and third, and I saw a man like the Sophoclean horse, for though seeming sluggish from age, he recovered a youthful impulse in his studies. He died at home, having lived seventy years, and was buried in a certain suburb of his own, in which he had most of all lived.

Nor will I pass over Marcus the sophist of Byzantium, on whose account I might even rebuke the Greeks, if, being such a man as I shall show, he should not yet meet with the reputation that is his own.
