Now Marcus traced his descent to the ancient Byzas, and his father, of the same name, had slaves who worked the sea at Hieron — and Hieron is by the mouth of the Pontus. His teacher was Isaeus, from whom, having learned to expound according to nature, he adorned it with a graceful gentleness. A most adequate example of Marcus's style is the Spartan advising the Lacedaemonians not to receive those who came naked from Sphacteria. For he began this theme thus: "A Lacedaemonian who has kept his shield to old age — gladly would I have killed these naked men." And what sort of man he was in his discourses too one may gather from this: for teaching about the art of the sophists, that it is manifold and varied, he made the rainbow an example of his argument, and began the discourse thus: "He who has looked upon the rainbow as a single color has not looked upon it so as to marvel; but he who saw how many colors it has, marvelled the more." Those who attribute this discourse to Alcinous the Stoic err both about the style of the speech and about the truth, and are the most unjust of men in robbing the sophist also of what is his own.

Antipater the sophist had as his fatherland Hierapolis, which is to be reckoned among the prospering cities of Asia, and as his father Zeuxidemus, of the most distinguished there; and having frequented Adrianus and Polydeuces, he was fashioned more after Polydeuces, relaxing the impulses of his thoughts by the rhythms of his expression. Having heard Zeno the Athenian too, he learned from him precision about art. Being an improviser he did not neglect studied works either, but he went through Olympic and Panathenaic orations for us and took into his history the deeds of the emperor Severus, by whom especially being appointed to the imperial correspondence, he sounded forth something brilliant in it. For let it be declared by me that, while many studied and composed better than this man, none wrote letters better, but, like a brilliant actor of tragedy who understands the drama well, he uttered things worthy of the royal person. For what he said had clarity and greatness of judgment, and the expression from what was at hand, and with pleasure the asyndeton, which especially makes a letter brilliant.

The character of his brows and the thoughtfulness of his face declared Marcus a sophist; for indeed he was always considering something in his mind and training himself in the things that lead to extempore speaking. And this was shown by the set of his eyes, fixed for the most part upon secret thoughts, and was confessed by the man himself; for when one of his friends asked him how he had declaimed the day before, he said, "Worthily of speech before myself, but less so before my pupils." And when the man wondered at the answer, Marcus said, "I make active use even of silence, and two themes exercise me, and three under the one that I argue in public." His beard and hair he kept in a squalid state, on which account he seemed to the multitude more rustic than befits a man of understanding. This is just what Polemo the sophist experienced toward him; for Marcus came into the lecture room of Polemo, being already renowned, and as those who had come to the hearing sat together, one of those who had sailed to Byzantium recognized him and signified it to his neighbor, and he to the next, and it was passed round to all, that he was the Byzantine sophist; on which account, when Polemo asked for themes, all turned toward Marcus that he might propose one. And when Polemo said, "Why do you look at the rustic? For this man will not give a theme," Marcus, raising his voice as was his custom, and lifting up his head, said, "Both will I propose, and will declaim." Thereupon Polemo took him up, and understanding that he spoke in the Dorian manner, discoursed at the man much and marvellously, trusting to the moment; and having declaimed, and having heard the other declaim, both was admired and admired in turn.

Being enrolled among the consuls, he governed the nation of the Bithynians, but seeming to use the sword too readily he was relieved of the office. The life of Antipater was sixty-eight years, and he was buried at home; and he is said to have died by endurance rather than by sickness. For he was considered the teacher of the children of Severus, and we used to call him "teacher of gods" in the praises of his hearing; but when the younger of them died on a charge of plotting against his brother, he wrote to the elder a letter containing a monody and a dirge, saying that one eye out of two was his, and one hand, and that those whom he had taught to take up arms for one another, these he heard had been taken up against one another. That the emperor was provoked by this let us not disbelieve, for these things would provoke even a private man who wished his seeming to have been plotted against not to be disbelieved.

After this Marcus came to Megara — and the Megarians are colonists of the Byzantines — and the Megarians were at faction with the Athenians, their minds at the height of bitterness, as though the decree against them had just been written, and they would not receive them when they came to the Lesser Pythian games. But Marcus, coming forward among them, so transformed the Megarians that he persuaded them to open their houses and to receive the Athenians, with their wives and children. Hadrian the emperor too admired him when he came on an embassy on behalf of the Byzantines, for of the emperors of old he was the most disposed to foster excellence.

Polemo the sophist was neither, as most suppose, a Smyrnaean, nor, as some say, of Phrygian stock, but Laodicea in Caria brought him forth, a city neighboring the river Lycus, inland, but more powerful than the cities on the sea. The house of Polemo includes many of consular rank, and still does; and his lovers were many cities, but above all Smyrna; for these, having from his youth discerned something great in him, brought together upon the head of Polemo all the crowns in their gift, voting to him and to his family honors enviable in their city, for they granted to the man and to his descendants the right to preside at the Hadrianic Olympic games, and to embark on the sacred trireme. For in the month of Anthesterion a trireme is sent aloft into the market-place, which the priest of Dionysus, like a steersman, guides as it looses its cables from the sea.

Much in the circle of the sophists is Hermocrates the Phocaean too sung, having shown strength of nature beyond all whom I interpret; for though he kept company with no marvellous sophist, but had heard Rufinus of Smyrna, who in sophistical matters dared rather than succeeded, he interpreted most variously of the Greeks and both understood and arranged, not some themes but not others, but once for all all that were declaimed; for indeed he handled well the figured themes too, devising very many ambiguities and mingling the signified with the suppressed.

While he was teaching at Smyrna, he benefited the city in these ways. First, he made the city appear more populous than itself, since youth flowed into it from continents and islands, not undisciplined or a mingled mass, but choice and pure Greece. Next, he made it dwell in concord and free from faction; for in former time Smyrna was in faction, and those of the upper city were at variance with those by the sea. He was of the greatest worth to the city in his embassies too, going before the emperors and contending in advance for her interests. Hadrian, at any rate, who was attached to the Ephesians, he so won over to the Smyrnaeans that in a single day he poured out upon Smyrna ten million drachmas, from which both the grain-market was built and a gymnasium, the most magnificent in Asia, and a temple visible from afar upon the headland, which seems to lie opposite Mimas. And further, by rebuking their public faults and by admonishing them most wisely, he was of benefit, and he likewise rooted out insolence and all arrogance, the more so because he did not even disaccustom them from Ionian ways. He benefited them in these matters too, no doubt: the suits they had against one another he did not allow to go forth anywhere else, but settled them at home. I mean the suits about money; for those against adulterers and temple-robbers and murderers, from the neglect of which pollution grows, he urged not only to bring out but to thrust forth from Smyrna, for they needed a judge with a sword. And the charge brought against him by the multitude — that when he travelled many beasts of burden followed him, and many horses, and many slaves, and many breeds of dogs for various kinds of hunting, while he himself rode in a chariot drawn by some Phrygian or Celtic team with silver bridles — this won renown for Smyrna; for a city is made brilliant by its market and the magnificent furnishing of its buildings, but it is made brilliant also by a prosperous house; for not only does a city give a man a name, but it also wins one for itself from a man. Polemo cared also for Laodicea, frequently visiting his own house there and benefiting it in public matters as much as he could.

His grandfather was Attalus, the son of Polemo the sophist, and his father Rufinianus of Phocaea, a consular man, who married Callisto the daughter of Attalus. When his father died, he came into so implacable a quarrel with his own mother that Callisto did not even let fall a tear over him when he died in his youth, when indeed even to the bitterest enemies the things of youth seem piteous. And this, to one who hears it thus, will rather attach to the wickedness of the youth, if not even his mother suffered anything over him; but to one who reckons the cause, and that he ceased to love his mother over her love for a slave, the youth would appear to be in accord with the laws, which have granted even the killing on such charges, and she would appear worthy to be hated even by those not akin, over the things by which she shamed both herself and her son.

His honors from the emperors were such as these. Trajan the emperor granted him to travel free of charge by land and sea; Hadrian extended this to all his descendants, and enrolled him too in the circle of the Museum for the Egyptian maintenance; and at Rome, when twenty-five myriads were demanded, he paid over this money although Polemo had neither said that he needed it nor given prior notice that he would give it. And when Smyrna accused him of having laid out for his own pleasure much of the money bestowed on them by the emperor, the emperor sent a letter composed thus: "Polemo has rendered me an account of the money bestowed on you by me." Even if someone shall call this an act of pardon, it surely was not possible for him to find that pardon over the money except by his preeminence in the rest of his virtue. And when the emperor had consecrated the Olympieum at Athens, completed after five hundred and sixty years, as a great achievement of time, he bade Polemo too pronounce the hymn over the sacrifice. And he, as was his custom, fixing his eyes upon the thoughts already presenting themselves, gave himself up to his speech, and from the foundation-platform of the temple discoursed much and marvellously, making the opening of his speech the statement that his impulse concerning it had not come without the gods. The emperor reconciled to him also his own son Antoninus, in the handing over of the scepter when he was becoming a god from a mortal. What this was, I must make plain. Antoninus governed all Asia together, and lodged in the house of Polemo as the best in Smyrna and that of the best man; but Polemo, coming home by night from abroad, cried out at the doors that he was suffering grievously, being shut out of his own house, and then he compelled Antoninus to remove to another house. The emperor knew of this, but asked nothing about it, that the wound might not be reopened; rather, considering the times after his own and that often those who attend upon and provoke even gentle natures call them forth, he feared for Polemo; on which account, in his testament concerning the empire, he said, "And Polemo the sophist was the counsellor of this my purpose" — by this preparing in abundance the way to obtain pardon, as for a benefactor to whom thanks were due. And Antoninus jested with Polemo about the affairs at Smyrna, indicating, no doubt, that he had not forgotten them, but by his honors on each occasion he raised him to greatness, giving a pledge, as it were, that he did not remember them. He jested thus: when Polemo came to the city, Antoninus embraced him and said, "Give Polemo a lodging, and let no one cast him out of it." And when a tragic actor, from the Olympic games in Asia over which Polemo presided, said that he was appealing, since he had been driven out by Polemo at the beginning of the play, the emperor asked the actor what hour it was when he was driven from the stage, and when he said that it happened to be midday, the emperor very wittily said, "But me he drove out of his house about midnight, and I did not appeal."

But just as Hermocrates escapes this charge, so he could not escape that one; for the deep paternal estate handed down to him he squandered, not on rearing horses or on public services, from which one may even raise a name, but on unmixed wine and companions such as to provide matter for comedy too, such as those once provided who flattered Callias the son of Hipponicus.

Let these things stand as a showing of a gentle emperor and a high-spirited man. For Polemo was so high-spirited that he discoursed with cities from a position of superiority, with potentates without abasement, and with the gods on equal terms. For when he displayed extempore speeches to the Athenians, on the occasion of his first coming to Athens, he did not set himself to praise of the city, many as are the things one might say on behalf of the Athenians, nor did he speak at length about his own reputation, although such a style too is profitable to sophists in their displays; but knowing well that one must check rather than exalt the natures of the Athenians, he discoursed thus: "They say, men of Athens, that you are wise hearers of speeches. I shall find out." And when a man who had ruled the Bosporus and had been fashioned in all Greek education came, in his study of Ionia, to Smyrna, Polemo not only did not place himself among his attendants, but, when the man begged to keep company with him, repeatedly put him off, until he forced the king to come to his doors, bringing with him ten talents as a fee. And when he came to Pergamon, at the time when he was sick in his joints, he slept in the temple, and when Asclepius stood beside him and bade him abstain from cold drink, Polemo said, "My good sir, what if you were treating an ox?"

When Antipater had now come into the imperial correspondence and was eager to join his own daughter, who was poorly off in appearance, to him, Hermocrates did not leap toward that man's prosperity, but, when the matchmaker led the conversation to the power of Antipater, which he then had, he said that he would never be a slave to a large dowry and to the pride of a father-in-law. And when his kinsmen pushed him into the marriage and considered Antipater "Corinth of Zeus," he did not yield until Severus the emperor, having sent for him to the East, gave him the girl, when indeed, one of his friends asking him when he would hold the unveiling, Hermocrates most wittily said, "The veiling, rather, taking such a one." And not long after he dissolved the marriage, seeing her neither pleasant to look at nor suited in character.

This greatness and loftiness of spirit he drew from Timocrates the philosopher, having kept company with him for four years when he came to Ionia. And it is not amiss to make Timocrates too known. This man was from the Pontus, and his fatherland was Heraclea, whose people praise the customs of the Greeks; and at first he philosophized about the medical kind of discourse, knowing well the doctrines of Hippocrates and Democritus, but when he had heard Euphrates of Tyre, he let himself go with full sails into that man's philosophy. He was so much more choleric than was moderate that, as he discoursed, his beard and the hair on his head used to rise up, like those of lions in their charges. His tongue was easy and vehement and ready, on which account he was of the greatest worth to Polemo, who welcomed such an impetuosity of speech. At any rate, when a quarrel arose for Timocrates with Scopelianus, on the ground that he had given himself over to pitch and to hair-pluckers, the youth that frequented Smyrna was divided, but Polemo, hearing both, became a partisan of Timocrates, calling him the father of his own tongue. And when he was making his defense to him over the speeches against Favorinus too, he shrank back warily and submissively, like those boys who fear the blows from their teachers if they have committed any disorder.

The emperor too, having become a hearer of Hermocrates, admired him equally with his grandfather, and allowed him to ask gifts; and Hermocrates said, "Crowns and immunities and maintenances and purple and the priesthood my grandfather handed down to us his descendants, and what should I ask of you today that I have had for so long? But since it has been enjoined upon me by the Asclepius at Pergamon to eat partridge fumigated with frankincense, and this spice is now so scarce among us that barley meal and laurel leaves are fumigated to the gods, I need fifty talents of frankincense, that I may serve the gods and be served myself." The emperor gave the frankincense with praise, saying that he blushed because he had been asked for little.

This same submissiveness he used toward Scopelianus too at a later time, when he was chosen to go on an embassy on behalf of the Smyrnaeans, and asked, as for the arms of Achilles, for that man's persuasiveness. With Herodes the Athenian he kept company partly from submissiveness, partly from a superior position. How this too came about I wish to make plain, for it is noble and worthy of remembrance. Herodes was passionately fond of extempore speaking, more than of being thought a consul and of consular descent; and not yet knowing Polemo, he had come to Smyrna to keep company with the man at the time when he himself was setting in order the free cities. Embracing him and greeting him warmly, at the same moment as he took his mouth from his mouth, he said, "When, father, shall we hear you?" And Herodes supposed that he would put off the hearing, saying that he shrank from running the risk before such a man; but Polemo, with no pretense, said, "Hear me today, and let us go." When he heard this, Herodes says he was astounded at the man, that his tongue too was extempore, and his judgment. This shows the high spirit of the man, and, by Zeus, the wisdom with which he used the astonishment; but the following shows his self-control and decorum: for when Herodes came to the display, Polemo received him with long praise, worthy of the words and deeds of Herodes.

Hermocrates was assisted in his displays, first, by the glory of his grandfather, for human nature welcomes more the excellences passed down from fathers to children, on which account an Olympic victor from a house of Olympic victors is more glorious, and a soldier from non-unsoldierly stock more noble, and the pursuits of a father's and forebears' house are more pleasant, and inherited arts are better; and he was assisted too by the bloom about his appearance, for he was charming and statuesque, as youths are, and the boldness of the youth among the multitudes brought astonishment to the many, with which men are astonished at those who do great things without anguish. There contributed too his fluency and the ring of his tongue and his discerning the themes in a point of time and the matter read and spoken being more ancient than for a young man to conceive and expound. The declamations of Hermocrates are about eight perhaps, or ten, and a certain speech, not long, which he delivered at Phocaea in the Panionian bowl. And let it be declared by me that none would have out-resounded the tongue of this youth, had he not been deprived of advancing to manhood, caught by envy. He died, according to some, at twenty-eight, but as some say, at twenty-five, and his father's land received him, and his father's tombs.

The stage-manner of the man, which he used in his declamations, one may learn both from Herodes, in one of his letters to Varus, and I too will make it plain from there. He came to his displays with a relaxed and confident countenance, but he was carried in on a litter, since his joints were already destroyed. And he considered his themes not in public, but withdrawing from the crowd for a short time. His voice was brilliant and intense, and a marvellous resonance rang out from his tongue. Herodes says too that he leaped up from his chair at the climaxes of his themes, so great was the impulse that overflowed in him, and that when he had rounded off a period, he brought the final clause of it with a smile, indicating how much he spoke without effort, and that he pawed the ground in the passages of his themes no less than the horse of Homer. He says that one hears him on the first day as a judge does, on the next as lovers do, and on the third as those who marvel do — for indeed he kept company with him for three days. Herodes records too the themes upon which he kept company with him. The first, then, was Demosthenes swearing off a bribe of fifty talents which Demades was bringing against him, on the ground that Alexander had sent word of it to the Athenians from the accounts of Darius; the next was breaking up the Greek trophies, the Peloponnesian war having come to a settlement; the third of the themes was bringing the Athenians, after Aegospotami, back into their demes. Concerning this Herodes says that he sent him fifteen myriads, calling them the fee for the hearing, and that when Polemo did not accept it, he himself thought he had been slighted, but that Munatius the critic, who was drinking with him — and this man was from Tralles — said, "Herodes, it seems to me that Polemo dreamed of twenty-five myriads, and thinks himself the less by that amount by which you did not send so much." Herodes says that he added the ten, and that Polemo took them eagerly, as one recovering a debt. Herodes granted Polemo this too — not to come forward before him to a display of speeches, nor to contend against him, but to drive out of Smyrna by night, lest he should be forced; for he thought it bold even to be forced. And throughout the rest of his time he continued to praise Polemo and to set him beyond wonder; for at Athens, having contended brilliantly in the contest about the trophies, and being admired for the impetus of his speech, he said, "Read the declamation of Polemo and you will know a man." And at Olympia, when Greece cried out over him, "You are one like Demosthenes," he said, "Would that I were like the Phrygian" — so naming Polemo, since at that time Laodicea was reckoned with Phrygia. And when Marcus the emperor said to him, "What do you think of Polemo?" Herodes, fixing his eyes, said, "The din of swift-footed horses strikes about my ears" — indicating, no doubt, the resounding and high-sounding quality of his speeches. And when Varus the consul too asked him what teachers he had used, he said, "Under this one and that I was taught, but under Polemo I was already teaching."

Polemo says that he heard Dio also, having made a journey for this purpose to the nation of the Bithynians. Polemo used to say that the works of prose writers must be carried out on the shoulders, but those of the poets in wagons. And the following too is among the things that bring honor to Polemo. Smyrna was in dispute about the temples and the rights attaching to them, having made Polemo her advocate when he had now come to the end of his life. But when he died at the very impulse of the journey on behalf of these rights, the city fell to other advocates, and as they argued the case poorly in the imperial court, the emperor, looking toward the advocates of the Smyrnaeans, said, "Was not Polemo appointed advocate to you for this contest?" "Yes," they said, "if you mean the sophist." And the emperor said, "Perhaps, then, he composed some speech on behalf of the rights, seeing that he was to contend before me and over such great matters." "Perhaps, O Emperor," they said, "but not for us to know." And the emperor granted adjournments to the suit, until the speech should be brought; and when it had been read in the court, the emperor gave judgment in accordance with it, and Smyrna went off victorious in the precedence, and they said that Polemo had come back to life for them.

Since of distinguished men not only the things said in earnest are worthy of record, but also those said in their lighter moments, I will record too the witticisms of Polemo, so that not even these may appear to have been passed over. An Ionian youth was living luxuriously at Smyrna beyond the ways of the Ionians, and deep wealth was destroying him, which is an evil teacher of undisciplined natures. The youth's name was Varus, and, corrupted by flatterers, he had persuaded himself that he was the fairest of the fair, and taller than the tall, and of those about the wrestling-school the noblest and most skilled, and that not even the Muses would strike up more sweetly than he, whenever he turned to singing. He thought much the same about the sophists too, for he supposed that he could ride past even their tongues whenever he declaimed — and declaim he did — and those who borrowed money from him used to add to the interest the obligation of hearing him declaim. Polemo too was being brought under this tribute, while he was still young and not yet sick, for he had borrowed money from him; and since he did not pay court to him, nor go to his hearings, the youth was difficult and threatened "notices." Now the "notices" are a written warning of the market, announcing a default judgment against the man who does not pay. So when Polemo's relatives blamed him as disagreeable and ill-tempered, since, when it was in his power not to be dunned and to make profit from the youth by giving him a kindly nod, he did not do this, but called him forth and provoked him, hearing such things he went to the hearing; but when, late in the afternoon, the declamation was proceeding and no harbor of the speech appeared, and everything was full of solecisms and barbarisms and contradictions, Polemo leaped up and, holding out his two hands, said, "Varus, bring on your notices." When a proconsul was racking a brigand who had been convicted on many charges, and said he was at a loss what penalty might be worthy of the man's deeds, Polemo, happening to be by, said, "Order him to learn old things by heart." For although this sophist had learned very much by heart, he nonetheless considered learning by heart the most toilsome of the things in his training. And seeing a gladiator streaming with sweat and afraid of the contest for his life, he said, "You are in such anguish as if you were about to declaim." And meeting a sophist who was buying sausages and sprats and the cheap kinds of fish, he said, "My good fellow, it is not possible for one who feeds on these to play well the part of the high spirit of Darius and Xerxes." And when Timocrates the philosopher said to him that Favorinus had become a chattering thing, Polemo most wittily said, "And so has every old woman" — mocking his eunuch-like nature. And when an actor of tragedy, at the Olympic games in Asia, pointed to the earth at the words "O Zeus," and at "and Earth" raised his hand to heaven, Polemo, who was presiding over the games, drove him out of the contest, saying, "This man has committed a solecism with his hand." No more about these things; for even these suffice to make plain the charm of the man.

The style of Polemo's speeches is warm and full of contest and ringing clear, like the Olympic trumpet; and there shines upon it too the Demosthenic quality of judgment, and his dignified expression is not supine, but brilliant and breathing, as though from the tripod. Those, however, are mistaken about the man who say that he handled invectives best of the sophists, but defenses less well; for this argument is shown to be untrue both by this theme and that among those in which he makes a defense, but most of all by the Demosthenes who swears off the fifty talents. For having arranged a defense so difficult, he proved sufficient to the speech with amplitude and art. I see the same error also in those who think that he was carried away in the figured themes, hindered in his course as a horse in difficult ground, and that he excused himself from them with the very maxims of Homer: "For hateful to me as the gates of Hades is the man who hides one thing in his heart and says another." For this perhaps he said hinting and intimating the difficulty of such themes; but he contended best in those too, as is shown by the adulterer who is unveiled, and the Xenophon who claims to die for Socrates, and the Solon who asks to wipe out his own laws when Peisistratus had received his bodyguard, and the three Demosthenes speeches — the one presenting himself after Chaeronea, the one who seems to assess his own penalty at death over the Harpalus affair, and the one advising flight upon the triremes when Philip was advancing, although Aeschines had ratified a law that whoever mentioned the war should die. For in these most of all the themes brought forward by him in figured fashion, reins have been thrown upon the speech and the conceptions preserve their double meaning.

When he was often submitting to the physicians, as his joints were forming stones, he used to urge them, "Dig and cut the quarries of Polemo." And writing to Herodes about this disease, he wrote thus: "I must eat — I have no hands; I must walk — I have no feet; I must suffer pain — then I have both feet and hands." He died at about fifty-six years; and this measure of life, which to the other sciences is the beginning of old age, is to a sophist still youth, for this science, as it grows old, ripens wisdom. There is no tomb of his at Smyrna, even if several are spoken of; for some say that he was buried in the garden of the temple of Virtue, others not far from this by the sea, and there is a small temple and in it a statue of Polemo arrayed as he celebrated the rites upon the trireme, beneath which they say the man lies; others say in the courtyard of his house beneath the bronze statues. But none of these is true; for if he had died at Smyrna, he would not have been deemed unworthy of any of the marvellous temples among them, so as not to lie in it. But the following is truer: that he lies at Laodicea by the Syrian gates, where indeed the tombs of his ancestors are, and that he was buried while still living; for this he enjoined upon his dearest friends, and, lying in the tomb, he urged those who were closing the grave, "Bring it on, bring it on; let not the sun behold me silent." And to his relatives who were lamenting him he cried out, "Give me a body and I will declaim." With Polemo the things of Polemo came to an end; for those who came after him were indeed his kinsmen, but not such as to be examined against his excellence, except one man, of whom I shall speak a little later.

Nor let us forget Secundus the Athenian, whom some called "the splinter," as a carpenter's son. Secundus the sophist, then, was extraordinary in understanding, but unelaborate in exposition; and having educated Herodes, he came to a quarrel with him when he was already teaching, on which account Herodes used to jeer at him, adding the words, "Potter is angry with potter, and carpenter with orator." But when he died, Herodes both pronounced a speech over him and shed tears, although he died an old man. Worthy of remembrance about this man are several things, but most of all this theme: "Let him who began a faction be put to death, and let him who stopped a faction have a reward; the same man both began and stopped it, and asks for the reward." This theme he abridged thus: he said, "Well then — what came first? The stirring up of the faction. What second? The stopping of it. Having paid, then, the penalty for what you did wrong, take, if you can, the reward for the good you have done." Such was this man; and he is buried near Eleusis, on the right of the road to Megara.

A most renowned man too is Heracleides the Lycian, both in his affairs at home — since he was born of good fathers and became high priest of the Lycians, and the office, being that of a not great nation, the Romans deem worthy of great things, I think, on account of an ancient alliance — but Heracleides was more renowned in sophistical matters; for he was sufficient to understand, sufficient to expound, and unencumbered in his contests, and he did not over-frenzy in his panegyrical conceptions.

Cast out of the chair at Athens, when the companions of Apollonius of Naucratis combined against him, of whom the first and middle and last was Marcianus from Doliche, he turned to Smyrna, which of all cities most sacrifices to the Muses of the sophists. That the Ionic and Lydian youth and that from Phrygia and Caria ran together to Ionia for his company is not yet great, since Smyrna is near the door of all of them; but he drew the Greek world from Europe too, and drew the young from the East, and drew many Egyptians, who were not without a hearing of him, since he had contended in wisdom with Ptolemy of Naucratis in Egypt. He filled Smyrna, then, with a brilliant throng, and benefited it in many other things too, which I will make plain. A city turned toward many strangers, and especially those in love with wisdom, will both deliberate temperately and hold its assemblies temperately, guarding itself, no doubt, against being caught base among many and serious men, and it will care for its temples and gymnasia and fountains and colonnades, that it may appear sufficient to the throng. And if the city be also a shipowner, like Smyrna, the sea will give them many and abundant things. He contributed to Smyrna also in adornment, fitting up a fountain of oil in the gymnasium of Asclepius, of golden roof, and he held among them the eponymous office of the crown-bearer, from which the Smyrnaeans give names to their years.

Under Severus the emperor they say that he broke down in an extempore speech, fearing the court and the guards. But this, if some man of the market-place suffered it, might even incur a charge, for the tribe of the market-place is reckless and bold; but a sophist, busy with youths for the most part of the day, how could he hold out against astonishment? For an extempore speech is checked by a hearer with a grave face, and by slow praise, and by not being applauded in the accustomed way; and if he should perceive too an envy lurking against him, as Heracleides then suspected that of Antipater, he will both conceive the less and be the less fluent, for such suspicions are a darkening of judgment and a fettering of the tongue.

He is said to have cut down sacred cedars and to have had most of his estate confiscated, when indeed, as he was leaving the court, his pupils followed him consoling and supporting the man, and when one of them said, "But no one will take away your declamation, Heracleides, nor the glory from it," and recited over him the line, "One alone, I think, is still detained in the wide—" he said "fisc," most wittily having played upon his own ills.

He is thought, most of the sophists, to have acquired his science by toil, his nature not granting it to him; and there is a not unpleasant studied work of his, a moderate book, which is entitled "An Encomium of Toil"; and holding this book in his hands he met Ptolemy the sophist at Naucratis, who asked him what he was studying, and when he said it was an encomium of toil [ponos], Ptolemy, asking for the book and rubbing out the pi, said, "It is time for you to read the name of the encomium" — [onos, "ass"]. And the discourses too, which Apollonius of Naucratis delivered against him, attack him as sluggish and laboring.

The teachers of Heracleides were Herodes, among those not truly believed, and Adrianus and Chrestus among the genuine; and let us not disbelieve that he heard Aristocles too. He is said to have had a hollow belly and to have eaten very many dainties, and this gluttony settled into nothing for him. At any rate he died over eighty years, sound in body, and his tomb is said to be in Lycia; he died leaving a daughter and freedmen not serious, by whom the "Rhetoric" too was inherited; and the "Rhetoric" was a ten-talent farm of his at Smyrna, bought from his hearings.

Let no one consider Hippodromus the Thessalian second to the aforesaid sophists, for he appears better than some, and from some I do not know in what he falls short. Now Hippodromus had as his fatherland Larissa, a prospering city among the Thessalians, and as his father Olympiodorus, who surpassed all the Thessalians in rearing horses.

Though to have presided even once over the Pythian games seemed great in Thessaly, Hippodromus presided twice over the Pythian contests, and surpassed those above him in wealth and in the adornment about the contest and in greatness of judgment and in a justice that awarded the prize to the straight and right. At any rate, what was done by him about the tragic actor has left no surpassing to another in justice and judgment. For Clemens of Byzantium was a tragic actor such as no one yet in the art, but winning at the time when Byzantium was being besieged, he used to go away failing of the victory, that a city which had taken up arms against the Romans might not seem to be proclaimed through one man. And when he had contended best in the Amphictyonic contests too, the Amphictyons voted against the victory in fear of the aforesaid charge, but Hippodromus, leaping up with impulse, said, "Let these men fare well, perjuring themselves and judging against justice, but I give the victory to Clemens." And when the other of the actors appealed to the emperor, the vote of Hippodromus won repute again, for indeed the Byzantine won at Rome too.

Such as he was toward the multitudes, with marvellous gentleness he came to his displays. For taking over the art self-loving and boastful, he neither ever set himself to his own praise and checked the excesses of praises; at any rate, when the Greeks once shouted over him many words of good omen and even likened him to Polemo, he said, "Why do you liken me to the immortals?" neither taking from Polemo the being considered a divine man, nor giving to himself the being likened to such a one. And when Proclus of Naucratis composed an abuse, not an embassy, against all who taught at Athens, and enrolled Hippodromus in this reviling, we expected to hear a speech composed against the echo of what had been said, but he, saying nothing base, went through a praise of good repute, beginning from the peacock the bird, as being raised on wings by the praise. So, then, was he disposed toward his elders, and those who had preceded him by much time and not much; and how he was toward his age-mates one may learn from the following. A young man, coming from Ionia to Athens, went through praises of Heracleides beyond what is bearable; so Hippodromus, seeing him at the hearing, said, "This young man is in love with his own teacher. It is good, then, to assist him with his beloved; for he might even go off with a windfall, having learned to praise." And having said this he went through a praise of Heracleides such as had not yet been spoken over him. And the tears over Diodotus the Cappadocian, and the putting on of black clothing over him, who had provided a nature suited to declamation but died as an ephebe, proclaimed Hippodromus a father of the Greek world, and one having a regard that some illustrious men should arise even after him. This he showed most of all at Olympia; for to Philostratus the Lemnian, his own pupil, twenty-two years old, who was tossing up an extempore speech, he gave very much of the praises of the art, both what one ought to say and not; and when Greece asked Hippodromus to come forward at once, he said, "I will not strip against my own bowels." And having said this he postponed the hearing to the day of the sacrifice. Let these things, then, stand as a demonstration to me of an educated man, kindly and gentle in character.

Holding the chair of the sophists at Athens about four years, he was carried away from it by his wife and his wealth, for she was the most energetic of women and a good guardian of money, and with both absent the estate dwindled. Yet he did not neglect to attend the festivals of the Greeks, but frequented them for displays and for not being unknown. And he appeared better in these things too because, even after ceasing to teach, he always studied. For Hippodromus learned most by heart of the Greeks who, after Alexander the Cappadocian, were fortunate in memory, and he read most after Ammonius the Peripatetic, for I have not yet known a man more learned in books than he. And Hippodromus neglected declamation neither when living in the country nor when travelling nor in Thessaly, but he called it a possession better than wealth, from the hymns of Euripides and of Amphion.

Though rather rustic in appearance, he nonetheless displayed an irresistible nobility in his eyes, looking both fierce and bright. This Megistias of Smyrna too says he observed in him, being considered second to none of the physiognomists. For Hippodromus came to Smyrna after Heracleides, never having come before this, and getting off the ship he went to the market-place, to meet anyone educated in the local matters. Seeing a temple and tutors sitting near it and attendant boys carrying loads of books in satchels, he understood that someone of the distinguished was teaching within, and he came in and, addressing Megistias, sat asking nothing. Megistias supposed that he would discourse to him about pupils, being perhaps a father or rearer of children, and asked for what he had come, and he said, "You will learn when we are by ourselves." So Megistias, dismissing the youths, said, "Say what you wish." And Hippodromus said, "Let us give each other our clothing in exchange" — and Hippodromus happened to have a cloak, the other a public-speaker's mantle. "And what sense has this for you?" said Megistias. "I wish," he said, "to make for you a display of declamation." So he thought him possessed in announcing these things and driven in his mind, but examining the casts of his eyes and seeing him in his right mind and steady, he gave the clothing in exchange and, when he asked for a theme, proposed to him the magician who claims to die because he could not kill a magician who was an adulterer. And as he sat upon the chair and, waiting a little, leaped up, the account of madness came over Megistias the more, and he thought the advantages a thunderstruck folly; but when he began the theme and said, "But myself, at least, I can—" he was carried out of himself with wonder, and running to him he begged to learn who he was. "I am," he said, "Hippodromus the Thessalian, and I have come to train with you, that I might learn through one man so educated the character of the Ionic hearing. But behold me through the whole theme." About the close of the speech there was a run by those educated in Smyrna to the doors of Megistias, the report being swiftly spread to all that Hippodromus was among them; and he, taking up the theme, handled with another power the conceptions already spoken, and coming forward into the assembly of the Smyrnaeans he seemed a marvellous man and such as to be recorded among those before him.

His discourses depended on Plato and Dio, but his declamations were vigorous after the manner of Polemo, and even more refreshing, and his fluency was like that which those who read without distress give to what is very familiar to them. When Nicagoras the sophist called tragedy the mother of sophists, Hippodromus, correcting the saying, said, "But I call Homer the father." And he was eager too, from Archilochus, to call Homer the voice of sophists, and Archilochus the breath. The declamations of this man are about thirty, perhaps, and the best of them are the Cataneans and the Scythians and the Demades who does not allow them to revolt from Alexander while he is among the Indians. There are sung too lyric strains of his, for indeed he laid hold of the lyre of the lawgivers. He died at about seventy, both at home and leaving a son sufficient to preside over a farm and a house, but disordered and out of his wits, and uneducated in the things of the sophists.

Let those who deem Varus of Laodicea worthy of mention themselves not be deemed worthy of mention, for he was cheap and gaping and silly, and shamed what good voice he had with the twists of songs, to which one of the more licentious might dance. As to his teacher or hearer, why should I write, why should I tell, knowing well that none would teach such things, and that to those who have learned them the hearing of such things is a reproach?

Quirinus the sophist had as his fatherland Nicomedia, and a lineage neither of good repute nor again condemned, but a nature good at taking up learning and better at handing it on, for he practised not only memory but also clarity. This sophist was epigrammatic, and not copious about the thetic passages, but vigorous and vehement and clever at shaking the ears of a hearer, for indeed he improvised; but seeming more suited to accusations, he was entrusted by the emperor with the tongue of the treasury, and coming into power he seemed neither oppressive nor boastful, but gentle and like himself, nor money-loving, but, just as the Athenians sing that Aristides, after the imposition of the tributes and the islands, returned to them in his former cloak, so too Quirinus came back to his own ways, dignified by poverty. When those of the informers in Asia blamed him as more gentle about the accusations than they themselves instruct, he said, "And indeed it is far better that you take on my gentleness than that I take on your cruelty." And when they informed against a not great city for many myriads, Quirinus won the suit much against his will, and the informers, coming up to him, said, "This suit will raise you great, coming to the ears of the emperor." And Quirinus said, "It is fitting not for me, but for you, to be honored for having made a city uninhabited." Over a son who died, when his relatives consoled him, he said, "When shall I appear a man, if not now?" Having been a hearer of Adrianus, he did not agree with all his sayings, but there were some that he even struck out as not rightly said. The term of his life was the seventieth year, and his tomb is at home.

Philiscus the Thessalian is connected by descent to Hippodromus, and he presided over the chair at Athens for seven years, being deprived of the immunity belonging to it; and how this came about it is necessary to make plain. The Eordaean Macedonians, having proclaimed Philiscus for their local public services, as though this belonged to them over all who were sprung from their mothers, summoned him; the suit, then, coming before the emperor — and it was Antoninus, the son of the philosophic Julia — he was sent to Rome to settle his own affairs, and attaching himself to the geometers and philosophers about Julia, he obtained from her, through the emperor, the chair at Athens. But he, just as the gods are made by Homer to grant things to one another not all willingly but some even unwillingly, so indeed grew savage and was harsh toward him as one who had gone round about him; and when he heard that there was a suit of his too, of which he himself would be the hearer, he bade the man appointed over the suits to give him notice not to contend through another, but through himself. And when he came into the court, his walk gave offense, his stance gave offense, and his dress seemed not graceful and his voice half-womanish and his tongue supine and his looking somewhere else rather than at his thoughts; from these things the emperor, turning away to Philiscus, bridled him and throughout the whole speech let the water run upon him and made narrow questions in it; and when the answers of Philiscus did not match the questions, he said, "The hair shows the man, but the voice the orator," and after many such checks he set himself to the Eordaeans. And when Philiscus said, "You have given me immunity from public services by giving me the chair at Athens," the emperor cried out, "Neither you are immune nor anyone else of those who teach; for I would never, over little and wretched trifles of speech, deprive cities of those who are to perform their public services." Yet nonetheless even after this he voted to Philostratus the Lemnian immunity from public services for declamation, when he was twenty-four years old. The pretexts, then, for which Philiscus was deprived of being immune, were these; but let not the deficiencies about his glance and voice and figure deprive him of having Hellenized and composed in the best manner of orators. The style of his speech was talkative rather than competitive, but pure words shone through it too, and a novel ring. He died, then, leaving a daughter and a son of no worth, and the measure of his life was sixty-seven years. Though he had acquired at Athens a not unpleasant estate, he was not buried in it, but in the Academy, where the polemarch sets the contest over those buried from the wars.

Aelian was a Roman, but he Atticized, like the Athenians of the interior. This man seems to me worthy of praise, first, because he worked out a pure speech while dwelling in a city using another speech, and next, because, being called a sophist by those who grant such things as a favor, he did not believe it, nor flatter his own judgment, nor was he lifted up by the name, great as it is, but, having well examined himself as not suited to declamation, he set himself to composition and was admired from this. The general style of the man is simplicity, attaining something of the grace of Nicostratus, but it sometimes looks toward Dio and his tone.

When Philostratus the Lemnian once met him with a book still in hand, reading it with anger and intensity of voice, he asked him what he was studying, and he said, "I have worked out an accusation of the Wretch" — for so I call the lately deposed tyrant, since he shamed the affairs of the Romans with all licentiousness. And Philostratus said, "I would have admired you, if you had accused him while living. For to check a living tyrant is the part of a man, but to trample on one laid low is the part of anyone."

This man used to say that he had never travelled anywhere of the earth beyond the land of the Italians, nor embarked on a ship, nor known the sea, on which account he was deemed worthy of greater repute at Rome, as honoring its ways. He was a hearer of Pausanias, but admired Herodes as the most varied of orators. He lived above sixty years and died not leaving children, for he declined the begetting of children by never marrying. Whether this is happy or wretched is not for the present time to philosophize.

Since Fortune is most powerful over all human affairs, let not Heliodorus either be deemed unworthy of the sophists' circle, having become a paradoxical contest of Fortune. For this man was elected advocate of his own fatherland to the Celtic peoples along with another, and when the other fell sick and the emperor was said to be striking out many of the suits, Heliodorus ran to the camp in fear about his suit; and being summoned sooner than he thought, he tried to postpone to his sick colleague; but the man who summoned the suits, being insolent, did not allow this, but led him into the courts unwilling and dragging him by the beard. And when he came in and looked boldly at the emperor and asked time of the water, and managed the very deprecation cleverly, saying, "It will seem strange to you, greatest emperor, that one objecting to himself should contend alone in the suit, having no instructions," the emperor leaped up, calling Heliodorus "a man such as I have never yet known, a discovery of my own times" and such things, shaking his hand and the fold of his cloak. At first, then, an impulse to laugh fell upon us too, thinking that he was spitting upon him, but when he gave him the right to ride at public expense, and his sons, as many as he had, Fortune was admired as displaying her own strength through things so paradoxical, and much more was this shown from what followed. For when the Arabian understood that by some good spirit his affairs were advancing, he made full use of the emperor's impulse, like those shipowners who shake out the sails full in fair voyages, and said, "O king, grant me time for a display of declamation," and the king said, "I hear; and speak on this: Demosthenes, having broken down before Philip, and fleeing a charge of cowardice." And as he declaimed, the emperor not only provided himself well-disposed, but prepared the praise from others too, looking fearfully at those who heard without praise. And indeed he set him over the greatest of the advocacies at Rome, as more suited to courts and suits. When the emperor died, an island was assigned to him, but, taking a charge of murder on the island, he was sent up to Rome to make his defense to the commanders of the legions, and seeming clear of the charge, the island too was given back to him. And he grows old at Rome, neither courted nor neglected.

Aspasius the sophist was brought forth by Ravenna, and Ravenna by the Italians, and his father Demetrianus educated him, knowing well the critics of speeches. Aspasius was much-learned and much-heard, and praising novelty, but nowhere falling into tastelessness, from using what he knew in season. And this, no doubt, is best in music too, for the seasons of the tones gave a voice both to the lyre and the flute and taught melody. But devoting himself to expounding in approved fashion and with simplicity, he neglected breath and amplitude, and not having improvisation from nature, he secured it by toil.

He came too to many parts of the earth, both being with the emperor and moving about by himself. He presided over the chair at Rome, in his youth most of good repute, but growing old with the charge of not wishing to give way to another. The quarrel of Aspasius with Philostratus the Lemnian began at Rome, but grew greater in Ionia, increased by Cassianus and Aurelius the sophists. Of these the one, Aurelius, was such as even to declaim in taverns over the wine there, while the other was such as to be bold toward the chair at Athens through the occasions which he abused, but to teach no one except Periges the Lydian. About the manner of the quarrel I have spoken, and why should I again interpret what has been sufficiently shown? But that there is something good to be found even from an enemy was shown in many human affairs, but most of all in these men; for, being at variance, Aspasius gained for himself improvisation with fluency, since Philostratus was renowned in this part too, and the other in turn chastened his own speech, hitherto running wild, toward that man's precision.

The letter composed by Philostratus on how one ought to write letters is aimed at Aspasius, since, having come into the imperial correspondence, he wrote some letters more contentiously than was fitting, and others not clearly, neither of which befits an emperor; for an emperor, whenever he writes, needs not enthymemes nor arguments, but opinion, nor again obscurity, since he speaks laws, and clarity is the interpreter of law.

Aspasius, then, was a pupil of Pausanias, but not without a hearing of Hippodromus, and he was teaching at Rome already well advanced in age when these things were being written by me. So much about Aspasius. But concerning Philostratus the Lemnian — and what this man was in the courts, what in public speaking, what in compositions, what in declamations, how great in extempore speech — and concerning Nicagoras the Athenian, who was crowned herald of the Eleusinian temple, and Apsines the Phoenician, how far he advanced in memory and precision, it is not for me to write, for I would even be disbelieved as showing favor, since I had friendship with them.
